Vmatch is packaged in Bioconda (2.3.1), but its recipe declares license: Unknown / OTHER and the upstream site could not be reached when this was checked in July 2026, so its terms could not be established. With no measured gain and unverifiable terms, BacFlux does not use it.

docs.title: 9. Summary
docs.text:
Question Answer Are these independent callers? No. Shared MacSyFinder + ICEscan detection engine. Boundaries and clustering are independent. Detection, 30 curated elements BacFlux 20/30, MAP 17/30; MAP found nothing BacFlux missed Class, 17 shared elements Agree on 14; all 3 differences are ICEberg ICEs that MAP called IMEs Call burden, 40 genomes BacFlux 65 calls / 2.63 Mb (68 / 2.69 Mb with ICEscan on all 40); MAP 64 calls / 2.88 Mb Negative controls, 32.6 Mb 2 candidate calls each (BacFlux 5 with ICEscan on); identical coordinates on the one shared call Boundaries Comparable — chromosomal median |start offset| 5,141 bp vs MAP 7,427; standalone recovery 0.94 vs 0.94. §6.3 records that this comparison prompted two fixes to our att search Is vmatch required by BacFlux? No. Two implementations of the intended repeat search agreed on the 180 tested windows; this was not a direct Vmatch executable benchmark.

Nothing here supports a claim that either pipeline is better than the other. It supports three narrower claims: BacFlux's caller recovers the curated elements MAP recovers plus three more; it assigns the ICE/IME class in line with ICEberg's curation in the three cases where the two callers differ; and its boundary refinement is comparable to a vmatch-based refiner without requiring vmatch.

Every mobility statement derived from these calls remains a prediction. An element reported as predicted self-transmissible has conjugation machinery that looks intact; it has not been shown to transfer. The confirmatory experiment is a filter or broth mating assay, and no output of this module substitutes for one.

docs.title: 10. Citations and credit
docs.text:
The tools and resources this comparison depends on, credited plainly. Reading EBI's pipeline is how we found the ICEscan model set, which materially improved BacFlux's IME and AICE handling; that debt should be acknowledged in any publication.

  • EBI Mobilome Annotation Pipeline — ebi-metagenomics/mobilome-annotation-pipeline, v5.0.0, Apache-2.0. EMBL-EBI Microbiome Informatics team. https://github.com/ebi-metagenomics/mobilome-annotation-pipeline
  • ICEfinder2 — Wang M., et al. ICEberg 3.0: functional categorization and analysis of the integrative and conjugative elements in bacteria. Nucleic Acids Research (2024). ICEfinder2 provides the ICEscan models and the boundary- refinement approach MAP's ICEfinder2-lite implements.
  • CONJScan / MacSyFinder — Cury J., Abby S.S., Doppelt-Azeroual O., Néron B., Rocha E.P.C. Identifying conjugative plasmids and integrative conjugative elements with CONJscan. Methods in Molecular Biology (2020); and Abby S.S., Néron B., Ménager H., Touchon M., Rocha E.P.C. MacSyFinder: a program to mine genomes for molecular systems with an emphasis on CRISPR-Cas systems. PLoS ONE (2014).
  • Conjugation system classification — Coluzzi C., Garcillán-Barcia M.P., de la Cruz F., Rocha E.P.C. Evolution of plasmid mobility: origin and fate of conjugative and non-conjugative plasmids. Molecular Biology and Evolution (2022).
  • ICEberg (curated coordinates used as truth) — Wang M. et al., NAR (2024).
  • ICEBs1 discovery (the negative-control lesson, §6.2) — Auchtung J.M., Lee C.A., Monson R.E., Lehman A.P., Grossman A.D. Regulation of a Bacillus subtilis mobile genetic element by intercellular signaling and the global DNA damage response. PNAS (2005).

docs.title: Licensing position
docs.text:
No code from the EBI pipeline was copied or adapted. Three of its scripts — bin/ice_boundary_refinement.py, bin/map_tools/icefinder_process.py and bin/prescan_to_fasta.py — derive from ICEfinder2 and carry CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 headers. Their NonCommercial and ShareAlike conditions are incompatible with distribution under BacFlux's MIT licence, and making such code optional would not change that.

CONJScan and ICEscan models are fetched separately when enabled and are not bundled with BacFlux. Their attribution, NonCommercial and share-alike terms remain relevant to use and distribution. See Licensing.

Users can analyse the same assembly with MAP for a broader inventory. Check terms relevant to its outputs and source databases separately from the licence of BacFlux's implementation.

docs.title: Method reference: running CONJScan and ICEscan together
docs.text:
BacFlux can search for conjugation machinery with two model sets. This page explains how it combines their evidence when the optional ICEscan layer is enabled, what the second set added in the benchmark, and which profiles it excludes.

Terms used on this page

CONJScan the default model set, distributed with MacSyFinder. Conservative and well validated ICEscan the optional second set, a fork of CONJScan taken from ICEfinder2. Off by default; adds classes CONJScan cannot see MacSyFinder the engine both run on: it looks for a quorum of required genes, not single hits ICE integrative and conjugative element — moves itself between cells IME integrative mobilisable element — needs a helper element to move AICE actinomycete integrative and conjugative element, using a TraB-family translocase for DNA transfer T4SS type IV secretion system, the mating apparatus att site the short repeat marking an integrated element's ends MGE mobile genetic element, the general term IS insertion sequence, the smallest kind of mobile element HMM hidden Markov model, a statistical profile used to recognise a protein family

Measured on the 28 genomes of the benchmark set that carry a curated element. There are 30 such elements — 18 curated ICEs and 12 curated IMEs — but two genomes carry one of each, so 30 elements sit on 28 genomes (Validation). The 12 negative-control genomes are not used here, since this experiment scores what changes on genomes that contain something. Two arms, differing only by whether the ICE caller was given ICEscan's table (mobilome.icescan.run: true).

Short version. ICEscan is not a second opinion — it is a fork of the tool we already run. We add it alongside CONJScan, take only two things from it (integrase hits and the IME/AICE element classes), and ignore four of its integrase profiles because they are not element integrases. Measured effect: ICEs unchanged, IMEs meaningfully better, boundaries barely moved.

docs.title: ⚠ Read this before quoting any coordinate from this page
docs.text: The per-element coordinates and ratios in §8.1 and §8.2 are superseded and must not be quoted. A later rework of the att-site search moved many of them substantially: SPI-7 is listed below at 83,403 bp and is now called at 133,582 bp against a curated 133,500; ICEEc2 at 55,055 bp is now 92,237 bp. Current headline figures are on Validation and Head-to-head vs the EBI pipeline; the per-element tables behind them are not in the repository. Both arms used the same att search when §8.1–8.2 were measured, so the comparison between them holds for that code. The census (§8.3), costs (§9) and uncurated-call table (§10) were re-measured for both arms on 2026-08-02.

docs.title: 1. What ICEscan is, and the correction that matters
docs.text:
ICEscan is the machinery-model set distributed with ICEfinder2 and used by the EBI mobilome-annotation-pipeline. The approach is theirs and the credit is theirs (§12).

Adding it to a workflow that already runs CONJScan does not give two independent opinions: ICEscan is a fork of CONJScan, by the same authors at Institut Pasteur, one minor version behind the release BacFlux installs. Its metadata.yml does not describe it as ICEscan at all:

maintainer:
  name: Charles Coluzzi Eduardo Rocha
  email: ccoluzzi@pasteur.fr erocha@pasteur.fr
short_desc: CONJScan - Models for detection of conjugative and mobilisable elements.
vers: 2.0.1
doc: https://github.com/macsy-models/CONJScan
license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0
copyright: 2018-2022, Institut Pasteur, CNRS

Its README.md is the CONJScan README verbatim, down to the macsydata install CONJScan instruction; MacSyFinder's run log calls the package ICEscan-2.0.1, and BacFlux installs CONJScan 2.1.0.

Two forks of one model set share their profiles, their scoring and most of their blind spots. Their agreement is largely structural, not independent corroboration; only their disagreements are used.

docs.title: 2. Exactly what ICEscan adds and removes
docs.text: Measured by diffing the two installed model directories.

docs.title: 2.1 System models
docs.text: CONJScan 2.1.0 ICEscan 2.0.1 Chromosome/T4SS_type{B,C,F,FA,FATA,G,I,T} 8 8 Chromosome/dCONJ_type* (decayed machinery) 8 0 — removed Chromosome/MOB (relaxase-only, mobilisable) 1 0 — removed Plasmids/* (the entire plasmid model set) 17 0 — removed Chromosome/IME absent 1 — added Chromosome/AICE absent 1 — added total definition files 34 10

docs.title: 2.2 Profile HMMs — 21 added, 1 removed
docs.text:
ICEscan carries 145 profiles against CONJScan's 125.

Added (21). Eight integrase/recombinase families — Phage_integrase, Recombinase, UPF0236, PB001819, rve, TIGR02224, TIGR02225, TIGR02249; the actinomycete AICE machinery — FtsK_SpoIIIE, RepSAv2, DUF3631, Prim-Pol; Gram-positive and IME-specific relaxase families — Relaxase_firmi_{MOBL,Rep_2,Viral_Rep_A,Viral_Rep_B1,Viral_Rep_B2}, Relaxase_PHA_IME_{A1,B}, Relaxase_profile_MOBT; plus T4SS_MOBL.

Removed (1). T4SS_MOBM.

The eight integrase profiles are the substantive addition: CONJScan 2.1.0 carries no integrase profile at all — conjugation machinery is its subject, not integration.

docs.title: 2.3 The mating-apparatus quorum is stricter in ICEscan
docs.text:
"Quorum" means how many machinery genes MacSyFinder must find, and how close together, before calling a type IV secretion system (T4SS — the apparatus that pushes DNA into the recipient cell).

CONJScan 2.1.0 chromosome T4SS ICEscan 2.0.1 T4SS min_mandatory_genes_required 3 4 min_genes_required 4–6 (varies by type) 8 (all types) inter_gene_max_space 60 genes 20 genes

ICEscan is stricter on every axis — on a fragmented or decayed element, the difference between a call and silence. That is why a swap loses elements.

docs.title: 3. Why we union rather than swap
docs.text:
A swap would trade CONJScan's MOB, dCONJ and plasmid models, and its looser T4SS quorum, for ICEscan's IME and AICE models. Per genome, that trade is bad:

genome curated element CONJScan hits ICEscan hits AF261825 SGI1 2 0 — genome emptied GU725392 ICEEc2 24 3 AL513382 SPI-7 24 3 AE009948 — 34 27 NC_004668_1 ICE_EfalV583_tRNALys 47 44

SGI1's genome goes to zero machinery hits under ICEscan alone: it is mobilised by a helper plasmid, its CONJScan signal is a MOB relaxase, and ICEscan deleted that model. ICEEc2 drops from 24 supporting hits to 3.

The union rule. Both model sets run at --coverage-profile 0.5 over the same Bakta proteins; the two best_solution.tsv tables are merged before the ICE caller sees them. From ICEscan we take only integrase anchors from four trusted profiles (§4) and the IME and AICE element classes. We never take its T4SS quorum, and we never use its system spans as element boundaries.

docs.title: 4. Four integrase profiles we deliberately do not trust
docs.text:
ICEscan's IME.xml lists eight profiles as interchangeable integrases. Four are not the integrase of an integrative element, and BacFlux excludes them: a hit to any of them is used as no anchor of any kind, neither integrase nor mating-pair component. This is not a claim that the proteins never take part in DNA mobility. The audit TSV records each exclusion with its reason (§4.2).

profile what the protein actually is why it must not anchor an element TIGR02249 IntI1, the class-1 integron integrase An integron is cargo inside elements, not the element. Measured casualty on CP042858.1: an att-bounded 32,103 bp tier-6 ICE became a 103,303 bp unbounded one, at unchanged high confidence, anchored on IntI1. Fires 4 times in best_solution.tsv on this set, every time as IntI1. TIGR02224 XerC, chromosomal dif-site recombinase Housekeeping: with XerD it resolves chromosome dimers at dif, and it is present in essentially every bacterial chromosome whether or not an element is, so a hit is no evidence of one. A XerC was measured being attached 43,639 bp from a 945 bp relaxase cluster, producing an element 6× its annotated size. TIGR02225 XerD, the other half of the same dif-site pair As XerC. rve the rve/DDE catalytic domain, shared by IS transposases A domain shared across different mobile-DNA proteins. Of its used hits, the overwhelming majority were proteins Bakta independently annotates as transposases (IS3 family ×16, IS6 IS15DIV ×14, IS6 IS1216E ×8). Anchoring on one turns any insertion sequence into a spurious element.

We diverge from upstream on rve on purpose. ICEscan's IME.xml lists rve as an exchangeable of Phage_integrase, so a reader comparing the two will find a real disagreement. rve is the DDE domain shared with IS transposases, which BacFlux detects separately; admitting it would double-count IS elements as IMEs. The audit text says so.

Trusted (4): Phage_integrase, Recombinase, UPF0236, PB001819.

docs.title: 4.1 A subtlety in how the exclusion is applied
docs.text:
MacSyFinder's best_solution.tsv has two gene columns. gene_name is the profile that matched; hit_gene_ref is the top-level model gene it stands in for. For a Recombinase hit these read:

gene_name = Recombinase        hit_gene_ref = Phage_integrase

Every excluded profile is an exchangeable of Phage_integrase, so filtering on hit_gene_ref would let all four back in. The caller gates on gene_name.

docs.title: 4.2 What was actually discarded, and how we know
docs.text:
Grepping the element table for profile names proves nothing — it never records them, so the grep returns zero either way. The evidence is the audit TSV. The caller writes one row_skipped | untrusted_integrase_profile row per genome in which an excluded profile matched, listing the hits per profile. On the 28 genomes of the ICEscan arm there are 15 such rows, recording 110 discarded hits:

profile hits discarded rve 103 TIGR02249 (IntI1) 5 TIGR02224 (XerC) 1 TIGR02225 (XerD) 1

Of these, 75 are rows of ICEscan's best_solution.tsv (71 rve, 4 TIGR02249). The other 35 are per-profile hits, which the caller reads on the three genomes where ICEscan assembled no system. None reaches an element.

Regression check, CP042858.1 — byte-identical in both arms:

4559721-4591823  len=32103  ice  bnd=denovo  conf=high
4911034-4988140  len=77107  ice  bnd=denovo  conf=high

The att-bounded 32,103 bp element survives at high confidence, and no 103,303 bp element exists anywhere in the set.

docs.title: 5. What ICEscan does not solve
docs.text:
It emits no coordinates. MacSyFinder reports gene ordinals, never base pairs. A row from the Tn4451 detection:

replicon  gene_name     hit_pos  model_fqn                locus_num
U15027    Recombinase   2        ICEscan/Chromosome/IME   1
U15027    T4SS_MOBV     6        ICEscan/Chromosome/IME   1

hit_pos 2 and 6 mean "the 2nd and 6th protein in the file". Every base pair BacFlux prints comes from its own join against the Bakta GFF3; the clustering, the coordinate work and attach_nearby_integrases cannot be delegated.

Its IME systems sprawl and are not loci. In IME.xml both mandatory genes (T4SS_MOBV and Phage_integrase) carry loner="1", exempting them from MacSyFinder's clustering. Counted across the 28 benchmark genomes in the best_solution.tsv files the caller consumes:

count ICEscan IME "systems" 54 …spanning ≤ 11 genes (usable as a locus) 22 …spanning > 1,000 genes 12 widest single "IME" 8,784 genes

Counted from best_solution.tsv, which is the file to quote: all_systems.tsv counts every candidate MacSyFinder considered rather than the ones it kept, and gives 97 / 33 / 24 for the same three rows. The widest single call, 8,784 genes in S. scabiei, is identical in both.

The widest is on NC_013929 (Streptomyces scabiei) and covers essentially the entire 10,148,695 bp chromosome as one "IME". BacFlux's clustering turns these into usable intervals.

It delimits nothing. ICEscan performs no att-site search. Every boundary comes from BacFlux's own att search, IS masking and tRNA scoring. Bounded fraction moves from 17/50 (34%) to 22/63 (35%) — essentially not at all.

The Bakta product-text regex stays a first-class source. Twelve of the 30 curated pilot elements have an integrase found only by INTEGRASE_PRODUCT_PATTERN matching Bakta's product text, with no usable ICEscan hit. It is not a fallback.

docs.title: 6. The coverage-threshold confound, stated plainly
docs.text:
--coverage-profile sets how much of an HMM profile a protein must cover to count as a hit. Lowering it finds more, and more marginal, hits — a genuine confound, easy to credit to the wrong cause.

We adopt 0.5 for both model sets. All 28 runs were verified:

28 × coverage_profile = 0.5   (ICEscan-2.0.1)
28 × coverage_profile = 0.5   (CONJScan-2.1.0)

The IME gain is 100% model set, not threshold. Tn4451 is detected through Recombinase + T4SS_MOBV as an IME system. Recombinase.hmm is one of the 21 profiles ICEscan adds, and CONJScan has no IME model at all — on the same genome it finds a single MOB relaxase hit and no integrase. No coverage threshold can make CONJScan find a profile it does not ship. The same holds for IME_CdiR20291_ND.

The ICE improvements seen at 0.3 are 100% threshold. They reproduce with plain CONJScan at 0.3 and no ICEscan at all. That arm is deliberately not used. Whether to lower the threshold is a separate question, separately measurable, and is not decided here.

⚠ To repeat the scored runs, use --coverage-profile 0.5 for both model sets.

docs.title: 7. AICE: mechanism and validation
docs.text:
An AICE (actinomycete integrative and conjugative element) is found in Streptomyces and relatives. It integrates into the chromosome like an ICE and does conjugate into another cell, but carries no relaxase and no mating-pair apparatus: a TraB / FtsK-SpoIIIE translocase moves it across as double-stranded DNA, where classical conjugation transfers a single strand nicked by a relaxase. Possoz et al. 2001 (PMID 11679075) concluded this for pSAM2 from differential SalI methylation, hedged as "probably transferred to the recipient as double-stranded DNA" but called "the first experimental evidence" for double-stranded transfer during conjugation. Vogelmann et al. 2011 (PMID 21505418) drops the hedge and measured the TraB pore at ~3.1 nm, wide enough for a duplex. (The translocase is TraB generically; pSAM2's copy is TraSA.)

An AICE does make single-stranded DNA, but not the kind that travels. It copies itself by rolling-circle replication inside one cell, and that intermediate is single-stranded (te Poele et al. 2008, PMID 18523858).

Tiers 5 and 6 are defined by a relaxase, plus a type IV secretion system for tier 6. An AICE carries neither, so the ladder has no tier for it. This is a limit of the tier scheme, not evidence that an AICE cannot transfer: an AMR gene inside an AICE keeps the tier its other evidence gives it, and the AICE is reported as context. Neither pilot set scores an AICE. ICEberg curates two AICEs on the benchmark's S. scabiei genome; at coverage 0.5 neither is recovered, and neither AICE call overlaps a curated element. Its exact output fields are:

field value element_type aice — never folded into ice mge_class its own class mobility_tier NA, never blank mobility_tier_reason explicit: "no tier: tiers 5 and 6 are DEFINED by relaxase + type IV secretion conjugation machinery, which an AICE does not carry…" mobility "predicted transferable into another cell as double-stranded DNA by a TraB translocase (FtsK/SpoIIIE family); not on the conjugation mobility ladder, whose tiers describe only relaxase + type IV secretion transfer" missing_components "none expected (an AICE has no relaxase and no mating-pair apparatus)" — so the row does not read as a degraded ICE

colocalise.py carries "aice" in both ELEMENT_TYPE_SYNONYMS and CONTEXT_ONLY_ELEMENT_TYPES; without both entries the class parses as None and logs "unrecognised element_type".

docs.title: ⚠ Validation status at coverage 0.5: zero
docs.text:
Two AICEs are called, both on NC_013929 (S. scabiei): 3,336,516–3,342,982 (6,467 bp, de novo boundary) and 5,262,523–5,273,184 (10,662 bp, unbounded). Neither overlaps any curated element, and neither pilot set contains a curated AICE. The one good AICE recovery on record — AICEScab56241, start +102 bp, end +44 bp, recovered fraction 0.99, the best boundary this caller has produced — exists only at coverage 0.3, not the arm we adopt.

So the AICE branch ships, and its validation on this benchmark is nil. Treat AICE calls as hypotheses.

docs.title: 8. Full before/after results
docs.text: Both arms differ only by --icescan-tsv. These are historical results from the original comparison. "Ratio" is called length ÷ published length; the descriptive band 0.4 ≤ ratio ≤ 2.0 is an evaluation convention, not proof of correct boundaries.

docs.title: 8.1 ICE pilot — 15/18 → 15/18, within the ratio band 9 → 9
docs.text:
element true bp control bp ratio union bp ratio boundary conf SXT(HN1) 19,086 — — — — missed R391 88,532 82,887 0.94 82,887 0.94 none high ICEKpnQD23-1 190,855 77,107 0.40 77,107 0.40 denovo high ICEEc2 93,895 55,055 0.59 55,055 0.59 denovo high ICE_EfmISMMSVRE1_Tn916 16,894 45,485 2.69 45,485 2.69 none high ICE(Tn4371)6061 43,841 43,585 0.99 43,585 0.99 none low CMGE(TZ080501) 125,779 62,749 0.50 50,425 0.40 none medium ICEKpn16_GR_13-1 151,942 148,839 0.98 148,839 0.98 tRNA high ICEMsp.M1D 199,376 39,437 0.20 39,437 0.20 none high ICEPsy10 161,009 — — — — missed ICEPvuChnBC22 148,751 51,523 0.35 51,523 0.35 none high ICEVflInd1 114,195 32,992 0.29 32,992 0.29 none low SPI-7 133,500 83,403 0.62 83,403 0.62 denovo high ICE_FprA2-165_rpsI 82,411 39,187 0.48 39,187 0.48 none medium ICE_EfalV583_tRNALys 138,318 26,040 0.19 26,040 0.19 denovo medium ICEB2 37,408 — — — — missed ICE_Step12228_tRNAser 38,415 24,222 0.63 24,222 0.63 denovo medium TR2 154,097 8,458 0.05 8,458 0.05 none medium

docs.title: 8.2 IME pilot — 3/12 → 5/12, within the ratio band 1 → 3 (original run)
docs.text:
element true bp control bp ratio union bp ratio conf IME_Sag2603_rpmG 522 — — — — missed MGIAmaMed1 1,248 — — — — missed IME_Ssal57I_tRNAlys 5,123 — — — — missed IME_CdiR20291_ND 5,551 — — 3,840 0.69 medium Tn4451 6,338 — — 5,942 0.94 low MTnPi10 7,591 6,252 0.82 6,252 0.82 medium IME_EfalV583_rpsI 9,405 — — — — missed IME_SsuNSUI002_NS 11,112 181,279 16.31 179,889 16.19 medium MGIVvuTai1 19,039 — — — — missed IME_FprA2-165_tRNAlys_2 23,194 — — — — missed SGI1 42,451 — — — — missed IMEMlNZP2037-1 110,480 8,164 0.07 8,164 0.07 medium

Both new detections fall within the stated ratio band rather than being oversized intervals that merely contain the curated element: Tn4451 at ratio 0.94 (start offset +75 bp) and IME_CdiR20291_ND at 0.69 (start offset +37 bp) — the two best-bounded IME recoveries the caller has produced.

With today's code the control arm (CONJScan alone) finds 2 of the 12, not 3. Its third detection, IME_SsuNSUI002_NS, was a 181,279 bp call laid over an 11,112 bp element. The scorer counts any overlap, so it passed. The union arm still finds 5, so the layer now adds three IMEs: the two above, and IME_SsuNSUI002_NS itself, now recovered as a 4,959 bp call starting 63 bp from its curated start.

docs.title: 8.3 Whole-set census (all 63 calls, not just scored ones)
docs.text:
Measured — both arms run over the same 28 genomes, the only difference being mobilome.icescan.run. Rates quoted in §5 predate the att-search rework and are higher in absolute terms; the comparison this page makes is unaffected, because restricted to ice-class calls the rate is identical in both arms (5 of 36, 14%).

control union total elements 51 63 ice 36 36 — unchanged ime 10 21 aice 0 2 conjugative_region 3 2 genomic_island 2 2 predicted self-transmissible 36 36 — unchanged confidence high 16 16 — unchanged bounded by a tRNA-anchored att pair 6 (12%) 8 (13%) … of ice-class calls only 5/36 (14%) 5/36 (14%) — identical

No element gained a self-transmissible claim. The net-new calls in the union arm are all IME or AICE — tier 5 or no tier.

"Bounded by an att pair" here means boundary_method=tRNA specifically, the only method the caller acts on: a denovo pair is reported but never applied to the coordinates (see Tuning). Restricted to ice-class calls, where a real element and a fragment are not conflated, the rate is identical between the arms — ICEscan neither helps nor hurts how often an ICE gets its true edges.

docs.title: 9. Costs — what got worse
docs.text:
Three of the four costs still hold; the fourth no longer occurs.

1. CMGE(TZ080501) loses 12,324 bp. On KX077897: 48,091–110,839 → 60,415–110,839; recovered fraction 0.4988 → 0.4009. With ICEscan on, an ICEscan Recombinase sits 0 bp from the cluster and wins the "then the closest" tie-break over a Bakta product-text Site-specific recombinase 11,032 bp away — and the more distant one was nearer the curated left edge. 0.4009 is about 110 bp from dropping out of the stated ratio band.

2. One boundary loss of two.

control union AE009948 929,751–986,650 · 56,900 bp · denovo · medium 923,639–941,160 · 17,522 bp · none · medium CP048437_1 150,670–187,352 · 36,683 bp · denovo · medium 158,404–187,352 · 28,949 bp · denovo · medium

On AE009948 the union arm loses the de novo boundary outright. On CP048437_1 both arms report denovo, so that element loses interval but not its boundary. high + boundary_method=none is 10 in both arms.

3. The nested double-report on CP011419.1 no longer occurs. The union arm once emitted a 179,889 bp ime candidate (98,234–278,122, ratio 16.19) with the 4,959 bp call (246,807–251,765, ratio 0.45, start +63 bp) nested inside it. It now gives three clean, non-overlapping calls — that 4,959 bp element, a compact 2,407 bp ime elsewhere on the same contig, and an unrelated ice — and no oversized candidate. A MacSyFinder loner gene (one admitted without the normal co-localisation test) was being treated as grounds to merge two distant clusters; that merge rule has been corrected.

4. Unscored ICE intervals shrink by 10–20 kb. Several loci not covered by either pilot move as ICEscan supplies a closer integrase — e.g. NC_004668_1 89,312 → 69,537 bp (2,177,344–2,266,655 → 2,197,119–2,266,655) at high confidence, CP048437_1 69,163 → 59,955 bp (1,318,921–1,388,083 → 1,328,129–1,388,083). These are unvalidated collateral of the same tie-break rule.

Open design question, not resolved here: when neither candidate integrase yields an att pair, is "then the closest" the right second key? It is what cost CMGE its 12 kb and what cost the AE009948 boundary above.

docs.title: 10. Limitations — read before trusting any output
There is no false-positive measurement, and this benchmark cannot produce one
docs.text:
score.py computes recall only — no precision, false-positive or specificity code at all, as its own docstring says. The scorer alone cannot resolve this: every genome in both pilots was chosen because it contains a curated element, so a call overlapping nothing curated may be a genuine second element rather than an error. Nothing here can tell the difference.

The table reports calls without curated overlap, rather than a false-positive rate. Measured against all 1,677 of ICEberg's curated entries on these 28 accessions, not just the pilots' 30 — the correct denominator for "does this call correspond to something curated":

calls overlap no curated element unvalidated self-transmissible unvalidated high control 51 17 (33%) 9 4 union 63 21 (33%) 9 4

In both arms, about a third of calls land on nothing curated, and nine predicted self-transmissible and four high-confidence calls lack curated overlap. The union does not worsen that ratio; it adds unvalidated IME and AICE calls at medium/low confidence on top of it.

docs.title: The negative control: two calls in 32.6 Mb
docs.text:
A negative control needs genomes with no reported ICE. Twelve closed genomes were screened, each verified absent from all 1,677 ICEberg entries:

Genome Why it is here Calls Buchnera aphidicola Sg / APS, Wigglesworthia glossinidia reduced endosymbionts, ~0.65 Mb, no MGE traffic 0 Prochlorococcus marinus, Synechococcus sp. CC9605 streamlined marine genomes 0 Aquifex aeolicus VF5 deep-branching thermophile 0 Staphylococcus aureus N315 clinical isolate, prophages + transposons 0 Escherichia coli K-12 MG1655 the most-studied bacterial genome there is 0 Pseudomonas aeruginosa PAO1 6.3 Mb reference strain 0 Halobacterium sp. NRC-1 an ARCHAEON — the models are bacterial, so a call would lie outside the intended bacterial-model scope 0 (3 with ICEscan) Bacillus subtilis 168 reference strain 1 ice Salmonella Typhimurium LT2 reference strain 1 ime

Total: two calls across 32,601,100 bp: one known ICE and one unresolved IME candidate. These counts are from the default machinery models alone. With the ICEscan layer on, the same genomes gave five calls: the same two plus three low-confidence cime_or_island calls on Halobacterium sp. NRC-1, built from integrase and type IV secretion profile hits with no assembled system.

B. subtilis 168 → ICEBs1, a real element, and the best-evidenced call in this validation: 529,362–549,932 (20,571 bp; ICEBs1 is ~20.5 kb), all four anchor classes, MOBT relaxase (NicK), boundary resolved by a tRNA-anchored att at tRNA-Leu(gag) — ICEBs1 integrates at trnS-leu2 — and Bakta annotated the integrase literally as "ICEBs1 integrase". ICEberg has no entry for NC_000964.3.

⚠ A warning about this benchmark's own design. The set originally justified including strain 168 with "ICEBs1 is absent from 168 itself". That is false: ICEBs1 was discovered in strain 168 (Auchtung et al. 2005). Had the call been counted rather than inspected, a textbook-correct detection would have been recorded as a false positive, and a working detector might then have been "fixed". Every call in a negative control must be examined, never merely counted.

Salmonella Typhimurium LT2 → 2,900,443–2,906,075 (5,633 bp): an integrase plus a protein Bakta labels only "DNA-binding protein", which CONJscan's T4SS_MOBM profile hits at i-eval 1.8e-84, coverage 0.986 — a near-full-length relaxase match. This combination supports an IME candidate but does not by itself establish a functional element. Whether this locus is a bona fide IME or two co-located genes is a specialist question; it is listed among the open domain questions rather than scored either way.

Interpretation. With the default models, ten of the twelve genomes produced no calls (nine with the ICEscan layer on), including large reference genomes containing recombinases, prophages and IS elements. It does not give a false-positive rate — "absent from ICEberg" is not "contains no element", ICEberg's curation being partial. The measured result with the default models is two candidate calls in 12 genomes, one explained by ICEBs1 and one unresolved. It does not establish zero false positives.

docs.title: Boundaries
docs.text:
About half of all calls are reported unbounded. On the union arm, 10 of the 20 detected curated elements (50%) carry an att pair; across all calls the rate is 34 of 63 (54%). The chromosomal median absolute offsets are 5,141 bp at the start and 14,912 bp at the end. Mind the denominator: 50% is over detected curated elements, 54% over all calls, and the two are different questions.

The arm comparison was made with the earlier att search, which has since been reworked. Under it, 6 of 18 detected elements carried a direct repeat in the CONJScan-only arm and 6 of 20 in the union arm, and on the nine ICE pilot elements that are both detected and chromosomal (the only ones where boundary error is a meaningful question — see the standalone-deposit note below) the median absolute offsets were 14,294 bp at the start and 34,239 bp at the end, identical in both arms: ICEscan moved boundaries not at all. That boundary comparison has not been repeated for the CONJScan-only arm since the search was replaced, so it holds only for the older search; likely, but not measured, for the current one.

Either way the shape of the problem is unchanged: half of all elements are reported unbounded, their start and end being the outermost machinery genes rather than the true edges, and the residual error on bounded ones is measured in kilobases. Read boundary_method before quoting any coordinate.

docs.title: One benchmark entry is broken
docs.text: SXT(HN1) / AB450045 is deposited as a 19,086 bp record containing 17 proteins, no relaxase and no T4SS, standing in for an element that is really ~100 kb. Both CONJScan and ICEscan return zero hits on it; no machinery-based caller can find machinery that is not in the record. It is counted as a miss throughout for consistency, so the highest achievable score on this pilot is 17/18.

docs.title: Other standing limitations
docs.text:
• ICEscan and CONJScan are forks of one another, so agreement between them is weaker evidence than agreement between independent tools would be (§1).
  • The AICE branch is entirely unvalidated at the adopted threshold (§7).
  • Two ICE pilot entries (ICEPsy10, ICEB2) are missed in both arms; seven of the eighteen ICE entries are "standalone" deposits where the element is the record, leaving no flanking sequence for an att site and making the boundary question trivial.
  • Agreement with ICEberg's coordinates is not the same as truth — several ICEberg entries are themselves predictions, or simply "the whole deposited record".

docs.title: 11. Licensing
docs.text:
The ICEscan models are CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (Institut Pasteur / CNRS) with a NonCommercial condition and attribution/share-alike requirements. This is the same licence as the CONJScan models the module already fetches.

BacFlux ships neither. Both are fetched at run time from a URL in config/config.yaml, default run: false, exactly as BacFlux handles its other opt-in databases: it ships the URL, never the data (see Licensing). Setting run: true means you download them under your own agreement with the licensor. Commercial users should leave this off or obtain permission from the model authors.

No ICEscan model, profile or code is present in this repository, and none of EBI's CC BY-NC-SA-derived scripts has been copied or adapted (see CITATIONS.md).

Reading their pipeline is how we learned that ICEscan existed, that it ships the IME and AICE models, and at what coverage threshold it is run. No code was copied — three of their scripts are CC BY-NC-SA-derived, and copying them would bring CC BY-NC-SA's NonCommercial and ShareAlike conditions into BacFlux, which are incompatible with its MIT licence (see Licensing). Adopting facts, parameters and design decisions is permitted, and is what was done.

Element ground truth

ICEberg 3.0 curated ICE/IME coordinates, as above.

docs.title: 13. Interpretation
docs.text:
Combining the model sets left ICE detection (15/18), predicted self-transmissible counts (36) and high-confidence counts (16) unchanged; IME detection goes 3/12 → 5/12 in the first run (2/12 → 5/12 with the current code, §8.2), with both new recoveries inside the 0.4–2.0 ratio band (0.94 and 0.69); all four integrase exclusions demonstrably fire; the CP042858.1 regression check holds byte-identically in both arms.

The integrase tie-break's second key ("then the closest", §9) is worth revisiting, and this benchmark still cannot measure a false-positive rate.

docs.title: The Medaka polishing model
docs.text:
This page explains how BacFlux selects a Medaka model, why the bacterial model can be appropriate for canonical basecalls from native bacterial DNA, and what the cited benchmarks establish.

Practical guidance

  • medaka_model: auto, the default, asks Medaka for the bacterial consensus model compatible with the basecaller recorded in the reads. If none resolves, the run stops before assembly.
  • The cited ten-genome comparison reported 26 residual errors with the bacterial model and 100 with the standard model. The benefit depends on the dataset.
  • Check assembly structure before polishing: missing replicons and unresolved circular overlaps can cause misleading read alignments.
  • For amplified DNA, set medaka_model to the standard model matching the basecaller (see Overriding the model). This rests on the bacterial model's stated scope; its effect on amplified libraries has not been measured.

The sections below describe the implementation and evidence separately.

Terms used on this page

ONT Oxford Nanopore Technologies, the long-read sequencing platform

docs.title: What BacFlux does
docs.text:
In long-read modes (nanopore, hybrid) with medaka_model: auto, BacFlux asks Medaka to resolve the model from the reads themselves, requesting the bacterial variant — workflow/scripts/12_medaka_check/medaka_model_check.py:

medaka tools resolve_model --auto_model consensus_bacteria <reads>

Medaka reads the basecall_model_version_id tag out of the FASTQ headers, maps it to the matching consensus model, and then substitutes the bacterial model — but only if the detected basecaller is on its compatibility list. On a typical R10.4.1 sup run this resolves to r1041_e82_400bps_bacterial_methylation.

That command is character-for-character what medaka_consensus itself runs for its --bacteria flag, so auto really does get the bacterial model — this is verified against the installed Medaka source, not inferred. If resolution fails (no basecaller tag, or a tag Medaka's lookup does not know) the check exits 1 with a suggestion table; it never falls back to a non-bacterial model. Model choice is worth that strictness: across ten genomes it was the difference between 26 and 100 residual errors (Wick 2025).

This happens in check_medaka_model (workflow/rules/shared/12_medaka_check.smk), which runs before assembly so a bad or incompatible model fails in seconds rather than after the assembler has spent an hour.

The same check puts the model's weights on disk. Medaka ships the weights of only a few models and downloads the rest from GitHub the first time they are needed: resolve_model above does that download as part of resolving the model, and an explicit name is followed by medaka tools download_models --models <name>. The check is a local rule, so on a cluster it runs on the computer that runs Snakemake, and the polishing job itself needs no internet.

Naming drift: dorado polish --bacteria

Wick's 2026 posts recommend dorado polish --bacteria in place of Medaka. As of his 2025-02-07 measurement the two shipped identical model weights, though he hedged that with "At the time of writing" and nobody has re-checked since. Noted only so the tool names in those posts do not read as a contradiction of this page; BacFlux stays on Medaka.

docs.title: Basecalling and polishing models
docs.text:
The objection assumes "methylation model" means the same thing at both stages. It does not — the two are different tools doing different jobs:

Dorado modified-base model Medaka bacterial model Stage basecalling consensus polishing Job reports methylation (MM/ML tags, per-base 5mC/6mA) corrects errors caused by methylation Effect on the A/C/G/T sequence none changes it Output an epigenetic annotation a more accurate consensus

The Medaka bacterial model is not the polishing counterpart of a Dorado modified-base model. It is a consensus model for ordinary canonical basecalls, specialised for the case where the template DNA is methylated.

The model-matching rule is still satisfied. Medaka models must match the error profile of the basecaller that produced the reads — ONT states this directly:

"it is important to specify the correct inference model, according to the basecaller used." — Medaka README (nanoporetech/medaka, v2.2.1)

The bacterial model declares compatibility with nine canonical basecaller models (hac and sup, v4.2.0 → v6.0.0; medaka/options.py, bact_methyl_compatible_models). There are no modified-base models on that list. If it required methylation-aware basecalling, it would name those instead. Medaka enforces this: an incompatible basecaller raises RuntimeError rather than silently polishing with the wrong model (medaka/models.py).

docs.title: Methylation-related consensus errors
docs.text:
The methylation errors exist because the basecaller was not methylation-aware. Bacteria methylate their own genomes (6mA, 5mC, 4mC, largely via restriction–modification systems). A modified base shifts the raw nanopore current away from the canonical signal, so a canonical basecaller — which can only emit A/C/G/T — misreads those positions systematically, at the same sequence motifs every time. Because the errors are systematic rather than random, more coverage does not remove them.

Those errors are already in the basecalls. The bacterial polishing model is trained to correct exactly that residue, which is why ONT scopes it to native material:

"For native data with bacterial modifications, such as bacterial isolates, metagenomic samples, or plasmids expressed in bacteria, there is a research model that shows improved consensus accuracy." — Medaka README (nanoporetech/medaka, v2.2.1)

ONT's own words: a research model, whose compatibility is deliberately broad — "compatible with several basecaller versions for the R10 chemistries".

In Dorado (checked against version 2.1.1 on 2026-08-21), modified-base calling writes modification probabilities beside the canonical calls and does not change which base is called. Basecalling with a modified-base model therefore leaves the same methylation-induced errors, and the same Medaka bacterial model still applies. The evidence and its limits are listed at the end of this page.

docs.title: Does it actually help?
docs.text:
The peer-reviewed measurement is Nagy et al. / NEKSUS Consortium (2026): 92 clinical Enterobacterales, R10.4.1 chemistry, Dorado sup v5.0.0 basecalls, assembled with Flye, Hybracter and Autocycler and polished with Medaka v2.

"Medaka polishing with un-subsampled long-reads resulted in small improvements in indels, but not SNVs for both Flye and Autocycler assemblies."

"Seven-locus multi-locus sequence type, antimicrobial resistance, virulence and stress gene annotation was equivalent across assembler/polisher combinations."

— Nagy et al. / NEKSUS Consortium (2026), Microbial Genomics 12(2):001631. https://www.microbiologyresearch.org/content/journal/mgen/10.1099/mgen.0.001631

Of the benchmarks cited here, it is the only one run on Flye assemblies, which is what BacFlux polishes: Wick's polishing comparisons are on Autocycler assemblies or deliberately degraded Raven drafts. In that dataset, polishing gave small improvements in indels and none in SNVs, and the assessed annotations were equivalent. These results do not guarantee unchanged typing, AMR or virulence calls for another dataset.

A smaller and earlier observation, on two bacterial genomes, compared Medaka v2 with the bacterial model against the previous release:

Genome Errors before Errors after Campylobacter lari 18 2 Enterobacter cloacae 11 10

Wick RR (2024) Medaka v2: progress and potential pitfalls. https://rrwick.github.io/2024/10/17/medaka-v2.html

Two genomes is a small sample, and the gain is variable — large on one, marginal on the other. The result does not establish a fixed benefit across organisms or preparations.

The largest tally is 147 assemblies, where the bacterial model improved 129 and made 6 worse (Wick 2026). The reported benefit was not universal. Assembly structure is one possible source of polishing errors, as described below; these counts alone do not establish the cause of every worsened assembly.

An older recommendation said the opposite, and is still findable

In October 2023, Wick tested Medaka on sup basecalls and concluded: "it performed erratically with the sup/res assemblies, making things worse more often than better", recommending "Use Medaka if you are assembling hac reads but skip it for sup/res reads" (post).

That test used r1041_e82_400bps_sup_v4.2.0 — the standard model. The bacterial model did not exist yet. Measured against each other on the same ten genomes, the standard model left 100 residual errors and the bacterial model 26, which is the gap that reverses the advice. The comparison supports the bacterial model for the native bacterial data tested. It does not establish a rule for every chemistry, basecaller or DNA preparation.

docs.title: Assembly structure and polishing
docs.text:
Unrelated to model choice: polish only structurally sound assemblies. In the 2024 post above, where small plasmids were absent from the assembly, their reads misaligned elsewhere and Medaka introduced over 100 erroneous changes. A missing replicon can therefore affect the sequence of other assembled replicons during polishing.

Wick broadened the warning in a 2025-02-25 revision of his assembly guide:

"Structural errors in your assembly (such as missing plasmids or start-end overlap of circular contigs) can sometimes lead to Medaka increa[s]ing the number of errors." — https://rrwick.github.io/2020/10/30/guide-to-bacterial-genome-assembly.html

So a missing plasmid is one case of a wider problem: an unresolved start–end overlap on a circular contig can also cause polishing errors. BacFlux's reorientation, plasmid-recovery and replicon-audit steps run before polishing partly for this reason.

docs.title: Overriding the model
docs.text:
The bacterial model assumes native, unamplified DNA. Amplification — ONT's PCR barcoding kit (SQK-RPB114.24) or a whole-genome amplification protocol — copies the template with unmodified bases, so the methylation the model corrects for is no longer there. If a library was amplified, pin the matched standard model instead of auto:

parameters:
  nanopore:            # or: hybrid
    medaka_model: r1041_e82_400bps_sup_v4.2.0

This is an example of a standard model; select one compatible with the actual basecaller. The 100-versus-26 comparison above was not an amplified-DNA benchmark and cannot quantify the cost or benefit of this choice on amplified libraries.

check_medaka_model validates any explicit name against the installed Medaka's model list, fetches its weights, and fails early with a suggestion table if the name is wrong. Amplification status cannot be read from the reads; it has to come from the lab record.

docs.title: Sourcing: what is documented, what is inference
docs.text:
Stated so the claims above can be defended or challenged individually.

Verified from primary sources

  • The consensus_bacteria call, and the early-validation rule — read from this repository (medaka_model_check.py, 12_medaka_check.smk).
  • The nine compatible canonical basecaller models, the substitution logic, and the RuntimeError on incompatibility — read from the installed Medaka 2.2.2 source (options.py, models.py).
  • "native data with bacterial modifications… improved consensus accuracy", "research model", "compatible with several basecaller versions", and the model-matching requirement — quoted from ONT's Medaka README (v2.2.1).
  • That --auto_model consensus_bacteria is the same call medaka_consensus makes for its --bacteria flag, and the exit-1-on-failure behaviour — read from the installed Medaka source and from medaka_model_check.py.
  • The 92-isolate Flye/Hybracter/Autocycler result and the annotation-equivalence statement — quoted verbatim from Nagy et al. (2026), cited above.
  • The error counts for C. lari and E. cloacae, and the small-plasmid pitfall — Wick (2024), cited above.
  • The broadened structural-error warning, and the 26-versus-100 residual-error figure for model choice — Wick (2025), cited above.

Inference, not quoted from documentation

  • The biological mechanism (6mA/5mC/4mC, restriction–modification systems, signal deviation at modified bases, motif-systematic errors that coverage cannot average out). Standard domain knowledge, but not taken from the sources above.
  • That amplified DNA is a contraindication. ONT scopes the model to "native data" but does not explicitly warn against amplified input. The caution above is read off that scoping, not quoted from a warning.
  • That methylation-induced errors are predominantly indels, and that frameshifted or pseudogene counts in the annotation are therefore a good readout for testing the model's benefit.

Not re-checked: whether dorado polish --bacteria still ships the same model weights as Medaka's bacterial model. Wick reported that in February 2025 and hedged it with "At the time of writing"; nothing here verifies it since.

Verified against Dorado 2.1.1, 2026-08-21. Modified-base calling does not feed back into which base is called, so it cannot repair a methylation-induced miscall and does not remove the need for this consensus model. Two independent lines establish it, and the SAM specification is consistent with it:

  • Dorado's basecall decoder emits only four symbols — alphabet = {'A','C','G','T'} in basecall/decode/beam_search.cpp. There is no symbol for a modified base. The modbase node reads the called sequence and writes only modification probabilities beside it; it never assigns to the sequence.
  • ONT's maintainers state the invariant outright, and treat it as a design constraint: "modification calling has no effect on the canonical basecall — you should get exactly the same sequence whether you do modbase or not. This is intentional" (dorado#1494, given as the reason for refusing a feature that would have let a modification probability alter the emitted base).
  • The SAM specification describes how modification annotations relate to the primary sequence: base modifications are "a series of edits from the primary unmodified sequence as originally reported by the sequencing instrument" (SAMtags), counted against the primary SEQ field. This format describes the output representation; it does not by itself prove how a basecaller uses modification information internally.

ONT's own documentation does not say this in words — it describes modified basecalling only as "an extension to the normal simplex and duplex basecalling subcommands" (https://software-docs.nanoporetech.com/dorado/latest/basecaller/mods/).

Two limits on the claim. It says no information flows back into base determination, not that output is byte-identical: enabling modification models changes GPU memory use and can shift the auto-selected batch size, and Dorado is not bit-reproducible across batch sizes — a difference that is non-determinism rather than feedback, and cannot systematically correct motif-specific errors. And it is specific to Dorado's split architecture; it does not hold for older basecallers where basecalling and modification calling happened inside one model.

docs.title: Method reference: hybrid mode on five closed genomes
docs.text:
Five bacterial isolates with published, high-accuracy reference genomes, run end to end through hybrid mode with every optional layer enabled. The genomes come from the Autocycler benchmark, where each was sequenced deeply on ONT and Illumina and assembled to a curated reference — providing an external reference for assessing assembly content and sequence.

Two things came out of it: a measurement of when short-read correction of long reads helps and when it does harm, and an end-to-end picture of what the workflow delivers on genomes with curated reference assemblies.

Terms used on this page

ONT Oxford Nanopore Technologies, the long-read platform IS insertion sequence — the smallest mobile element, and the main cause of contig breaks AMR antimicrobial resistance ICE integrative and conjugative element — carries its own conjugation machinery replicon one complete DNA molecule: a chromosome or a plasmid concatemer a circular sequence assembled as two or more tandem copies of itself

docs.title: The isolates
docs.text:
species reference replicons IS per Mb Illumina depth Providencia rettgeri 4,465,806 bp 2 1.8 102× Listeria innocua 2,972,545 bp 2 3.7 223× Enterobacter hormaechei 5,384,747 bp 4 7.4 92× Klebsiella pneumoniae 5,990,196 bp 5 15.7 82× Shigella flexneri 4,828,487 bp 8 81.2 67×

IS density is counted by the mobilome module on each finished assembly, so it is a number the workflow produces rather than one taken from the literature. It counts every ISEScan call, including the one or two look-alike calls described under Mobilome below.

The experiment used the published 50× ONT subsets

The full ONT sets published with these isolates reach 306×–1,070×, far deeper than routine isolate sequencing. The full-depth runs had short-read guidance on, and with guidance on hybrid passes Filtlong no --target_bases cap: Flye reported Assembled 0 disjointigs on all five genomes. The runs described here therefore use the 50× subsets published alongside the full sets, which is also the depth the original benchmark assembled.

With guidance off, the default, Filtlong caps the ONT reads at 500 Mb with --target_bases. With guidance on, subsample unusually deep ONT data before the run.

docs.title: Short-read correction of long reads: it can help, and it can lose a replicon
docs.text:
hybrid mode can give Filtlong the Illumina reads (-1/-2), so that it scores each long read by how well it agrees with them and trims (--trim) or splits (--split) it where agreement fails. That is what parameters.hybrid.short_read_guidance controls. Without it, Filtlong sees only the long reads: it filters on length and quality and caps coverage with --target_bases, which is also what nanopore mode does.

Three arms were assembled with Flye from the same 50× reads, differing only in the filtering before them:

arm filtering guided Filtlong with -1/-2, --trim, --split — short_read_guidance: true unfiltered none unguided Filtlong with --min_length, --keep_percent, --target_bases — short_read_guidance: false genome reference guided unfiltered unguided Providencia rettgeri 2 2c, +25 2c, +0 2c, +0 Listeria innocua 2 2c, −1,134 3c, +6,020 3c, +6,019 Enterobacter hormaechei 4 3c, −91,386 4c, −1,134 4c, +1,418 Klebsiella pneumoniae 5 4c, +2,274 4c, +2,281 4c, −1,234 Shigella flexneri 8 40c, −35,210 6c, +22,974 6c, +21,340

The unguided and unfiltered arms produced the same contig counts on all five genomes. This comparison points to the guidance options as the main source of the observed differences; it does not establish that length and quality filtering are harmless on other datasets. --split severs a read wherever 1,000 consecutive bases lack short-read support, and the regions where support thins are repeats and IS elements — the same regions whose spanning reads hold an assembly together. The severed fragments still pass --min_length, so mean read length and N50 both rise while contiguity collapses.

On Shigella, with 81 IS per Mb and the shallowest short-read coverage of the set, guidance turned a 6-contig assembly into 40. On Enterobacter it cost a whole replicon and 91 kb. On Listeria — the least repetitive genome, with by far the deepest short reads — it was the only arm to recover both replicons.

What can be said in advance, and what cannot

Five genomes cannot support a threshold. What they do show is a direction: guidance was harmful where IS density was high or short-read coverage was thin, and helpful on the one genome that was neither. Both quantities are measurable before assembly for the short reads, and only after assembly for IS density.

The practical reading: short-read guidance warrants particular scrutiny on repeat-rich genomes or shallow Illumina data. It is disabled by default. A fragmented ONT assembly should prompt comparison of the filtering arms and read support; fragmentation alone does not identify its cause.

docs.title: What the workflow delivered
docs.text:
Assemblies, against the published references. These runs had short-read guidance on. The table measures the delivered genomes, after polishing, whereas the arm comparison above measured the Flye assemblies, so total lengths differ from the guided column by up to 40 bp. The mobilome results that follow were produced from these delivered genomes.

genome contigs assembled difference Providencia rettgeri 2 4,465,802 −4 bp Listeria innocua 2 2,971,407 −1,138 bp Klebsiella pneumoniae 4 5,992,470 +2,274 bp Enterobacter hormaechei 3 5,293,335 −91,412 bp Shigella flexneri 40 4,793,237 −35,250 bp

Providencia differs in total assembly length by four bases from a reference built with Trycycler, Medaka, Polypolish and Pypolca. Equal or similar total length does not establish sequence accuracy. Two failure modes account for the rest, and both are worth recognising in your own data.

Small plasmids go missing. Klebsiella's reference carries a 1,240 bp plasmid and Enterobacter's an 80,745 bp one; neither survived. This is the documented small-plasmid loss of long-read assembly, described in att sites and small plasmids.

Small plasmids also arrive doubled. In the unguided arm, three of Shigella's six small plasmids assembled as tandem concatemers — 2 × 6,790, 3 × 3,181 and 4 × 3,835 bp, matching whole multiples to within 9 bp. A read longer than a small circle wraps it more than once, and the assembler represents that as a tandem repeat. The replicon then appears several times its true size and its genes more than once, so gene content and copy number read from it are wrong. Aligned against the reference, that assembly recovered three of the eight replicons as single contigs (the chromosome, the 222 kb plasmid and the 5,057 bp plasmid), three as concatemers, and lost the two smallest plasmids (2,088 and 1,240 bp). Total assembly length cannot separate these outcomes; only a per-replicon alignment can.

docs.title: Mobilome
docs.text:
Stage 08.mobilome with all four optional layers enabled:

genome AMR genes IS elements ICE/IME candidates named elements mobility tiers Listeria innocua 2 11 1 0 all tier 1 Providencia rettgeri 5 8 1 0 3 × tier 1, 2 × tier 6 Shigella flexneri 39 392 0 0 tiers 1, 2, 3, 5 Enterobacter hormaechei 44 40 4 2 10 × tier 1, 15 × tier 4, 19 × tier 6 Klebsiella pneumoniae 55 94 3 2 11 × tier 1, 44 × tier 6

The IS counts include ISEScan's look-alike calls over dnaA and over the chromosome's helicase loader, which the module removes before anything reads the IS table (see False IS21 calls over replication genes). On these genomes that is one call fewer for Providencia and two fewer for each of the other four. No AMR gene's tier and no ICE/IME candidate depends on those calls.

In these runs, L. innocua returned two tier-1 intrinsic candidates; this label does not establish species-wide intrinsic resistance. Klebsiella returned 44 genes with predicted self-transmissible context. Shigella had 392 IS calls, roughly four times the next-highest count. Repeat density is consistent with its assembly difficulty, but the count alone does not establish the cause of each contig break.

Enterobacter produced 15 tier 4 rows, all fifteen genes inside a single curated transposon, TnSMR478, on the chromosome — a stress- and metal-resistance cluster. Tier 4 requires the opt-in TnCentral layer, a curated element covering the gene, and no plasmid or ICE claiming it first (the mobility ladder), which is why it is rare; a single chromosomal transposon carrying fifteen genes satisfies all three at once.

Read that 15 as one element rather than fifteen findings. The other genome where tier 4 has been measured, ATCC BAA-2146, produced exactly one row from seven named elements, because six of the seven sat on plasmids and were claimed by tier 5 or 6 first (Worked example). The two results bracket the behaviour: the row count tracks genes, and how many rows an element yields is a property of the element.

docs.title: Acknowledgement
docs.text:
The isolates, the sequencing, the reference genomes and the read subsets are the work of Ryan Wick, Benjamin Howden and Timothy Stinear, published with the Autocycler paper and released on Figshare. BacFlux assembles with Flye alone and is not a competitor to a consensus assembler; where an assembly matters more than the analysis that follows it, a consensus assembly approach such as Autocycler may be appropriate. Its output can be analysed by BacFlux in contigs mode.

Wick RR, Howden BP, Stinear TP (2025). Autocycler: long-read consensus assembly for bacterial genomes. Bioinformatics 41(9), btaf474. https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btaf474

Data: https://figshare.unimelb.edu.au/projects/Autocycler/247142, released CC BY-NC 4.0. BacFlux ships none of it; the runs described here were made from a local download.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Each entry below gives the message you get, why it happens, and what to change.

Start with a dry run (-n). It checks workflow planning and many configuration errors before analysis jobs start, but does not validate all database contents or execute the tools — see Always dry-run first.

Terms used on this page

DAG directed acyclic graph — the job graph Snakemake builds from the rules, which decides what runs and in what order YAML the config file's plain-text format; indentation is significant and tabs are refused ONT Oxford Nanopore Technologies, the long-read sequencing platform GTDB Genome Taxonomy Database, the reference GTDB-Tk places each genome in

docs.title: KeyError: 'mode'
docs.text:
Symptom

The run stops as soon as the config is read, before the line naming the mode:

KeyError in file ".../workflow/rules/shared/00_common.smk", line …:
'mode'

Cause. The config has no mode: key, which is what selects the pipeline. It is read with bracket access on purpose (config["mode"], in the "Mode dispatch" section at the top of 00_common.smk), so a config without it stops the run rather than letting BacFlux guess a front end. A config written for an earlier release will not have it, and config/config_custom.yaml is git-ignored — a git pull never updates yours.

Fix. Back up your current configuration, then start from the shipped example and copy your database paths across by hand. The block layout changed as well, so read it rather than paste into it:

cp config/config.yaml config/config_custom.yaml

Details of what moved are in Coming from v1.

docs.title: A database path is wrong
docs.text:
Where a bad path is caught depends on which key it is, and the difference matters: some cost you seconds, one costs you the length of the run up to that rule.

Config key Caught What you see input.illumina_dir, nanopore_dir, contigs_dir parse time [BacFlux] input.contigs_dir is not an existing directory: '/no/such/dir' directories.vs2_db, antismash_db, dbcan_db, card_db, genomad_db parse time [BacFlux] directories.vs2_db is '/tmp', but it has no 'Done_all_setup'. Point it at the directory 'virsorter setup' produced … directories.checkv_db parse time [BacFlux] directories.checkv_db is '…', but that directory holds 0 CheckV database(s) (looking for */genome_db/checkv_reps.faa). links.dbcan_link, plus phix_link and card_link in the modes that need them parse time the missing key is named directories.blast_db DAG build (so, a dry run) MissingInputException in rule blob_json … affected files: <blast_db>/names.dmp, <blast_db>/nodes.dmp directories.bakta_db, eggnog_db, gtdbtk_db, platon_db not checked the tool fails when its own rule runs

Five of the six optional database keys share one check: a file that can only exist inside a real copy of that particular database — Done_all_setup for VirSorter2, aro_index.tsv for CARD, version.txt for geNomad, dbCAN.hmm for dbCAN, clusterblast/ for antiSMASH (function _resolve_optional_db_dir in 00_common.smk). A directory that exists but holds the wrong thing is therefore still caught. checkv_db is the exception, because it is the one key that points at the parent of the versioned database folder; it is checked for exactly one */genome_db/checkv_reps.faa underneath, so aiming a level too high or too low is caught as well (the CHECKVDB check in 00_common.smk).

Four of the five required databases are read, not verified

bakta_db, eggnog_db, gtdbtk_db and platon_db are taken from the config as given (the constants BAKTADB, DMNDDB, GTDBTKDB and PLATONDB in 00_common.smk; DMNDDB is eggNOG's). Set all four to paths that do not exist and a dry run still builds the whole job list without complaint; the failure comes later, inside Bakta, eggNOG-mapper, GTDB-Tk or Platon, which for the first three is an hour or more into the run. blast_db escapes this only because BlobTools reads names.dmp and nodes.dmp out of it, and those are declared rule inputs.

Check all five paths by hand before a long batch. What each one should contain is on Reference databases.

docs.title: Out of memory
docs.text:
BacFlux's two heaviest steps are the two that place genomes on a reference tree with pplacer: CheckM (completeness_and_contamination) and GTDB-Tk (taxonomic_assignment). pplacer's memory scales with its thread count and reaches tens of gigabytes.

Only GTDB-Tk hands pplacer BacFlux's thread count, through --cpus {threads} --pplacer_cpus {threads} (rule taxonomic_assignment in 30_taxonomy.smk). CheckM gets -t {threads} and no --pplacer_threads at all, so its placement runs at CheckM's own default of one thread, which is much the cheaper of the two.

{threads} in both rules is capped_cpus(24), which is min(resources.threads, 24) read from your config, and Snakemake lowers it again at run time if --cores is smaller (function capped_cpus in 00_common.smk). So if a run is still being killed there the lever is resources.threads, with --cores as a ceiling on top of it — see How threads reaches a rule. Lowering threads lowers pplacer's memory; it changes no classification setting that BacFlux passes to CheckM or GTDB-Tk.

The two rules are also kept apart on purpose: taxonomic_assignment declares CheckM's stats file as an input purely as a scheduling edge, so they never run on the same sample at once (its checkm_stats input, in 30_taxonomy.smk).

Never add --jobs alongside --cores

For a local run --jobs/-j is an alias for --cores, not a second "N jobs of M cores each" setting. Passing both switches the core budget off: two rules each declaring 8 threads, launched with --jobs 2 --cores 8, both got their full 8 threads and ran together. If your machine is far more loaded than --cores should allow, this is why. See --cores is the CPU budget.

eggNOG's --dbmem is the other memory lever, and it is off by default. Turning it on costs about 42 GB per concurrent job, and setting it with resources.ram_gb below that is refused at parse time rather than allowed to fail on the first job (the EGGNOG_DBMEM check in 00_common.smk). See eggNOG --dbmem.

docs.title: Databases on shared or network storage
docs.text:
Pointing BacFlux at a copy of a database that somebody else installed is supported and saves a great deal of downloading — every directories.*_db path is only ever read. Three things can go wrong with it.

The annotation crawls. eggNOG-mapper's annotation phase does random-access lookups into the 39 GB eggnog.db, once per seed ortholog. That phase is the slow tail of a run on any disk — it is why functional_annotation is routinely the last rule still finishing (the eggNOG --dbmem notes above EGGNOG_DBMEM in 00_common.smk) — and random access is the access pattern a network filesystem handles worst, so a shared copy is where it costs most. Either set parameters.eggnog.dbmem: true and accept the memory cost, or hold that one database on local disk. The trade-off is set out in Annotation.

CheckV's DIAMOND index belongs to whoever built it. CheckV's official archive ships no DIAMOND index; it is built locally after unpacking, and DIAMOND's format is versioned. Hand a shared copy straight to CheckV and it fails at [3/8] Running DIAMOND blastp search... DIAMOND task failed — after the contamination stage succeeded, which reads as a CheckV bug rather than an index mismatch. directories.checkv_db sidesteps this: BacFlux builds a local view — symlinks to the big read-only files, plus an index built by its own DIAMOND (rule checkv_db_local in 70_phage.smk; the reasons are set out above CHECKVDB in 00_common.smk). It costs ~950 MB once per output directory, and nothing is written to your copy.

Some files are readable by their owner and not by you. In a shared geNomad database, some small files, version.txt among them, can end up mode 0640 while the big data files beside them are world-readable. A file you may stat but not read passes an existence check and kills the run minutes later, so BacFlux tests every file in that directory for real read access at parse time, then names the first six offenders and counts the rest (the GENOMADDB check in 00_common.smk):

[BacFlux] directories.genomad_db is '/shared/db/genomad_db', but 9 file(s) in it are
not readable by you: <first six names> (and 3 more). geNomad needs all of them and
would fail partway through the run. Ask whoever owns that directory to make it
readable (chmod -R a+r), or point at a copy you own.

docs.title: medaka_model: auto cannot infer a model
docs.text:
Symptom

A long-read run stops at check_medaka_model, seconds after read filtering:

ERROR: Medaka could not work out a model from the reads. Medaka said:
…
ValueError: Input file did not contain precisely 1 basecaller model reference.

The message goes on to list the usual causes and the consensus models this Medaka version offers.

Cause. auto runs medaka tools resolve_model --auto_model consensus_bacteria over the filtered reads, which reads the basecaller model out of the FASTQ headers. Guppy and Dorado stamp it there; older data, re-headered data and much public data do not carry it at all. Read filtering is not the cause: Filtlong copies each FASTQ header unchanged, comment included, so if the filtered reads lack the basecaller tag, the raw FASTQ lacked it too. For such data auto cannot resolve a model.

The same check also stores the model's weights. Medaka ships the weights of only a few models and downloads the others from GitHub the first time they are needed. check_medaka_model is a local rule, so that download happens on the computer that runs Snakemake, and the polishing job, which on a cluster runs on a compute node, needs no internet. If that computer cannot reach GitHub, the check stops here as well: in auto mode the lines quoted from Medaka show the failed download, which the message lists among the usual causes, and for a named model the message reads Medaka model '…' exists, but its weights are not stored on this computer and could not be downloaded. Start Snakemake on a computer with internet, or set medaka_model: false to skip polishing.

Fix. Name the model explicitly, under the block named after your mode (parameters.hybrid for a hybrid run):

parameters:
  nanopore:
    medaka_model: r1041_e82_400bps_sup_v4.2.0

An explicit model can change the assembler as well

With flye_input_mode: auto (the default), the Flye read mode is chosen from the Medaka model name: a name containing fast selects --nano-raw, anything else --nano-hq. So setting medaka_model can change how the genome is assembled, not just how it is polished. To pin the polisher without touching the assembler, set flye_input_mode explicitly to nano-hq or nano-raw.

The failure is deliberately early: check_medaka_model runs right after read filtering and the assembler waits on its output, so a bad model costs seconds rather than surfacing after Flye has run. Both keys, and what auto accepts, are in Configuration.

docs.title: GTDB-Tk will not accept the reference database
docs.text:
Cause. GTDB-Tk hard-pins itself to one compatible reference release in its own source (COMPATIBLE_REF_DATA_VERSIONS). BacFlux pins GTDB-Tk 2.7.2, which requires GTDB R232, so an older release such as R220 or R226 is refused. GTDB-Tk makes the check itself, on startup, so the refusal lands in logs/taxonomic_assignment_{sample}.log rather than at parse time.

Fix. Download R232 fresh and point directories.gtdbtk_db at the release232 directory. There is no in-place upgrade, and taxonomy output cached from an older release should be treated as stale once that path changes. The download recipe and sizes are on Reference databases; why the two are pinned together is in Taxonomy.

docs.title: Half the genome left as contamination
docs.text:
Symptom

CheckM reports a badly incomplete genome that is not contaminated, and logs/select_contigs_{sample}.log carries the warning the selector prints whenever it drops more than 20% of the assembly, for example:

WARNING: decontamination is discarding 47% of the assembly (2,115,000 of
4,500,000 bp). If the kept assembly then looks incomplete but NOT contaminated,
the filter has most likely removed genome rather than contamination.

Cause. auto mode keeps one genus and drops every contig assigned to another. Which genus is set by decontamination.auto_vote: with bp, the default, the one whose contigs add up to the most base pairs; with contigs, the one carried by the most contigs. BLAST routinely scatters one organism across several related genus names, so the contigs that landed under a different name go, even though they belong to the same organism. On a contig count the risk is larger: many short contigs can outvote a few long ones, and on a long-read assembly the few long ones include the chromosome. If two genera tie exactly, the alphabetically first is kept, so the same input always gives the same answer. The curated alias table merges common splits such as Bacillus and Peribacillus, so whichever of the two wins the vote, the other is kept with it (the genus aliases). It covers only the splits it knows about.

Fix. Read 02.assembly/{sample}/contaminants/contig_taxonomy_decisions.tsv — every contig carries the reason it went — and {sample}_composition.txt beside it, which prints each genus's share of the DNA (bp) next to its share of the contig count (contigs). The vote follows the column auto_vote names, so when the two columns rank the genera differently, bp and contigs keep different genera. If you had set auto_vote: contigs, try the default bp first. Otherwise set decontamination.mode: include naming both genera, or mode: off, and re-run; Snakemake redoes only the affected steps.

The same folder holds {sample}_kept_genus.txt, the genus Bakta is given as the organism name: the kept genus that wins the same vote, counted over the kept contigs only. It is empty when no kept contig has a genus, and Bakta then runs without one.

If nothing survives at all, the rule fails

ValueError: No contigs were kept for sample 'X' with mode 'auto'.
Check taxonomy assignments and decontamination settings.

That is deliberate. An empty FASTA would let Snakemake mark the step complete and every stage from annotation onwards would run on no sequence. The decisions file is written before the check, so it is there to read.

docs.title: A plasmid is missing
docs.text:
Two independent steps can delete a real plasmid, and both have to be ruled out.

Step Why Where to look Decontamination The contig's genus comes from BlobTools' bestsum rule, which sums BLAST bit scores per taxon and so follows database composition rather than biology. A 2,014 bp K. pneumoniae plasmid was dropped as Escherichia because the summed BLAST bit scores favoured Escherichia (58,709) over Klebsiella (16,253), despite the known host contaminants/contig_taxonomy_decisions.tsv Long-read filtering filtlong ranks reads by quality and length, and short plasmid-derived reads can be disadvantaged by length weighting. Of the 603 ONT reads covering a 5,596 bp Col2 plasmid, keep_percent: 90 with length_weight: 10 keeps 93; the shipped keep_percent: 95 and length_weight: 1 keep 502 logs/filter_long_reads_{sample}.log

Recovering the reads is necessary, not sufficient

On that isolate no filtlong setting assembled the plasmid, raw unfiltered reads included. ONT ligation prep under-represents small circular plasmids by roughly four-fold, and no filter setting undoes that. keep_percent is the key to reach for; length_weight reaches filtlong only in hybrid mode, because the nanopore rule does not pass it.

A missing plasmid prediction does not establish that its sequence is absent from the assembly. Compare the assembly with an appropriate reference or inspect read and assembly-graph evidence before concluding that the replicon was lost. Both routes and their fixes are set out in Decontamination and Plasmids.

docs.title: The mobilome module cannot fetch its models
docs.text:
Symptom

The first run with mobilome.run: true fails at rule conjscan_models:

You reach the maximum number of request per hour to github.
Please wait before to try again.

Cause. The CONJscan models are not shipped with BacFlux; they are fetched at your request by msf_data install (macsydata install on older MacSyFinder), which reads https://api.github.com over an unauthenticated connection and turns the HTTP 403 you get for exceeding the hourly allowance into that message (class RemoteModelIndex in macsylib/model_package.py: its base_url, and its _url_json method). GitHub counts the allowance per IP address, so a shared machine or an institutional gateway can use it up without you making a single request yourself.

Fix. Wait, then relaunch. The rule fails rather than leaving an empty models directory behind, so nothing downstream runs on a model set that was never installed. The models land in 08.mobilome/conjscan_models/, are shared by every sample, and are never re-fetched for that output directory once they are there.

This is the only download the module always makes; the naming layers are opt-in, and they come from ordinary web servers rather than GitHub. Their rules check what came back, because a redirect to an HTML error page arrives with a 200 and would otherwise be indexed as an empty database that silently names nothing — so each one stops with an error and prints the first bytes it received. Turning those layers on is covered in Optional layers.

docs.title: A tool runs inside the workflow but not by hand
docs.text:
A few tools — QUAST and ISEScan among them — start with #!/usr/bin/env python, so when called directly they run under whichever python is first on the PATH, not the one in their own environment. Outside an activated environment that is usually the system Python, which has none of the tool's libraries, and the tool fails with an import error that looks like a broken install (QUAST reports a missing joblib3).

For rules with a declared conda environment, Snakemake activates that environment before the command when --sdm conda is used. To reproduce a step by hand, activate the environment first:

conda activate <path to the environment, under .snakemake/conda/ or your --conda-prefix>
quast ...

docs.title: Config (YAML) errors
docs.text:
Snakemake reports any config problem with one generic message:

WorkflowError:
Config file is not valid JSON or YAML. In case of YAML, make sure to not mix
whitespace and tab indentation.

That almost always means an indentation or list-syntax mistake, or a stray tab — not a problem with the values. Validate the file directly to get the exact line:

python -c "import yaml; yaml.safe_load(open('config/config_custom.yaml'))"

The key-by-key reference is in Configuration.

docs.text:
