  • Quick start — the first v2 run, start to finish.
  • Output files — what each numbered stage now holds.
  • Citation — which DOI to cite for work already published.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
To run BacFlux, obtain the repository, create a Snakemake environment and prepare the required reference databases. The repository contains the workflow rules, helper scripts and configuration template. Snakemake creates separate conda environments for the analysis tools used by the selected mode.

The instructions below cover the repository and software setup. Prepare the Reference databases before starting an analysis.

Terms used on this page

BAM the binary alignment file a read mapper writes

docs.title: 1. Get the repository
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/iLivius/BacFlux.git
cd BacFlux

A release archive from the repository's Releases page unpacks to the same tree. The clone is easier to keep current.

Four places in it matter:

Path What is in it config/config.yaml The configuration template: every setting of a run, commented in place. Copy it and edit the copy — never this file. workflow/Snakefile The entry point. It reads mode from your config and includes that mode's rule files plus the shared ones. workflow/rules/ The rules themselves, in shared/ and one directory per mode (illumina/, nanopore/, hybrid/, contigs/). workflow/envs/ 33 conda environment specifications, one per tool stack.

A fifth directory, .snakemake/, appears in whatever directory you launch from: it holds the conda environments Snakemake builds and its own bookkeeping. It is git-ignored, so it never ends up in a commit.

docs.title: 2. Create the launcher environment
docs.text:
conda create -n snakemake -c conda-forge -c bioconda snakemake=9.14.6
conda activate snakemake

Snakemake 9.14.6 or newer. That is the version BacFlux is tested with, and the Snakefile declares it as the minimum: an older Snakemake stops at once, before reading a single rule, with a message naming the version it needs. The pin in the command above gives you exactly the tested version.

This environment only runs Snakemake, which reads the configuration, plans the run and starts jobs; it holds no analysis software. Snakemake builds each tool's environment from workflow/envs/ itself, and a rule that has its own environment does not see tools added to this one.

docs.title: 3. What --sdm conda does
docs.text:
Every BacFlux run is started the same way, from the repository root:

# config_custom.yaml is your own copy of the shipped config/config.yaml
snakemake --sdm conda --configfile config/config_custom.yaml --cores 24

--sdm is short for --software-deployment-method, the modern spelling of --use-conda, which has been deprecated since Snakemake 8.4.7.

Each rule names an environment file in workflow/envs/ — the Bakta rules point at bakta.yaml, the Flye rule at flye.yaml, and so on. Snakemake works out which of them this run needs and builds them all before the first job starts, then reuses them on every later run. They are created under .snakemake/conda in the launch directory.

Two practical consequences:

  • The first run starts slowly. Solving and downloading a dozen or more conda environments takes minutes. After that they are on disk and the workflow starts straight away.
  • Tools never have to coexist. GTDB-Tk, antiSMASH, VirSorter2 and MacSyFinder each get their own environment, which reduces dependency conflicts between tools. The environments are pinned to different degrees: some to an exact version because a parser downstream depends on the output columns (ISEScan 1.7.3, MacSyFinder 2.1.6), others only loosely.

Only the environments your run actually needs are built

The Snakefile globs workflow/rules/<mode>/*.smk for the mode in your config, so an illumina run never solves the Flye or Medaka environment and a nanopore run never solves SPAdes. Several shared rules are gated the same way, on whether the run has short reads, long reads or reads at all.

Run Environments built Any mode blast, blobtools, quast, checkm, gtdbtk, bakta, antismash, dbcan, eggnog-mapper, abricate, platon, checkv, multiqc, python, download, and either virsorter or genomad illumina adds fastp, bowtie, spades, bbmap, qualimap nanopore adds nanoplot, filtlong, flye, dnaapler, medaka, minimap, qualimap hybrid adds everything in the two rows above, plus polypolish and snippy. Bowtie2 builds the first screen's coverage track; minimap maps the long reads for the second screen, over the delivered genome contigs adds minimap — its own front-end rule is plain awk, but BlobTools still wants a BAM, so the contigs are mapped against themselves mobilome.run: true adds isescan, macsyfinder, and tncentral for the optional naming and copy-number layers

docs.title: 4. The tools BacFlux expects to find, and does not install
docs.text:
Each analysis tool runs in a conda environment that Snakemake builds (section 3). Three things come from the computer instead, and BacFlux never installs them:

  • conda and the launcher environment with Snakemake (section 2);
  • bash, which Snakemake uses to run the commands of every rule;
  • the standard Unix command-line utilities. Rules call them for the small jobs around the analysis tools — creating folders, copying and linking files, checking a download — and, unless their own environment happens to include one, take them from the system PATH. The complete list is awk, basename, cat, chmod, cp, cut, date, dirname, find, grep, head, ln, ls, md5sum, mkdir, mv, rm, sed, sha256sum, sort, tail, tee, tr and wc. They belong to the coreutils, findutils, grep, sed and awk packages of every Linux installation; only a stripped-down system, such as a minimal container image, may lack some of them.

Download tools are the exception. A minimal Linux system can lack them — a minimal Debian or Ubuntu system has no wget, and a minimal Red Hat-family system no tar — so BacFlux provides them:

  • wget, tar, gzip and bzip2 come from workflow/envs/download.yaml (PhiX, CARD, dbCAN, the ICEscan models) or from the tool's own environment (geNomad, VirSorter2, CheckV);
  • curl and unzip come from workflow/envs/tncentral.yaml, for the optional mobilome layers (TnCentral, ICEberg, ISOSDB);
  • the CheckM package downloads its reference data (about 275 MB) while conda builds its environment, using the wget, tar and gzip in workflow/envs/checkm.yaml; building that environment therefore needs internet.

The download recipes on Reference databases, which you run yourself, use the wget and tar of your own system.

Rules without an environment. Eight rules declare no conda environment, and two more, all and download_all, are targets that run no command of their own. The eight run in the environment you launched Snakemake from and use only utilities from the list above:

Group Rules Uses Filter, copy or stage a FASTA filter_contigs, finalize_contigs, stage_qc_genomes awk, grep, head, cat, cp, mkdir, ls, dirname, tee Build a symlink view of a database you already hold download_amr_db_local, cazyme_db_local, secondary_metabolites_db_local, genomad_db_local, virsorter2_db_local mkdir, ln, basename

BacFlux's own helper scripts. Twelve rules — select_contigs, screen_final_contigs, build_replicons and nine rules of the mobilome module — run their script in workflow/envs/python.yaml, a pinned Python with nothing else in it. The scripts import only Python's standard library, so there is no pip install step.

The helper scripts' unit tests need nothing but Python and pytest, so they run from the launcher environment. pytest is not in the environment created above, so add it first:

conda install -n snakemake -c conda-forge pytest
pytest workflow/scripts miscellaneous -q    # three tests skip unless BACFLUX_TEST_* variables name real GTDB files

miscellaneous/ holds the workflow's own guard tests. They read the rule files and check, for example, that every helper rule names its Python environment and that every download rule is a local rule.

docs.title: 5. Reference databases
docs.text:
Five databases must be downloaded by hand before a run: Bakta, NCBI core_nt, eggNOG, GTDB and Platon. A further six may be pointed at a copy you already hold, and the rest BacFlux fetches itself on the first run that needs them, or all at once with the download_all target. Sizes, download recipes and the config keys that hold the paths are all on Reference databases.

Required database keys must exist and point to prepared databases. A missing key stops configuration parsing, whereas an empty or invalid path may fail later, when the database is used. For the six optional local-database paths, BacFlux also checks for an existing directory and database-specific files during planning. A successful dry run does not establish that every database is complete.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
This example runs BacFlux on Illumina paired-end reads. Prepare the required databases, obtain the repository, create the Snakemake environment and edit a copy of the configuration. Check the plan with a dry run before starting the analysis. For other input types, see Choosing a mode.

Terms used on this page

GTDB Genome Taxonomy Database, the reference used for taxonomic placement QC quality control 
# 1. Clone
git clone https://github.com/iLivius/BacFlux.git
cd BacFlux

# 2. Launcher environment (Snakemake only; the analysis tools are installed later,
#    per rule, by conda)
conda create -c conda-forge -c bioconda -n snakemake snakemake=9.14.6
conda activate snakemake

# 3. Make your own copy of the config, then edit the copy
cp config/config.yaml config/config_custom.yaml

# Continue with database preparation and configuration below before running BacFlux.

Run these from the repository root. workflow/Snakefile is found there automatically, which is why it never appears on the command line. Paths inside the config are used as you wrote them, so a relative one resolves against the directory you launched from, not against the config file — use absolute paths. output_dir is the exception: it is resolved to an absolute path for you.

Steps 1 and 2 in more detail, including which few rules run outside a conda environment: installation.

The config must be named on the command line

BacFlux ships no default configfile:, deliberately: Snakemake merges a hard-coded default with the file you pass, so a missing key in your copy would be quietly filled in from the shipped example — an empty database path, or a download link you did not choose — instead of stopping. Launching without --configfile gives you:

[BacFlux] No configuration supplied. Pass one explicitly, e.g.:
  snakemake --sdm conda --cores N --configfile config/config.yaml

docs.title: Before step 3 — five databases you supply
docs.text:
Five references are too large, or too tied to one release, for the workflow to fetch for you. You download them once and give BacFlux the path:

Config key Database Required database version directories.bakta_db Bakta v6.0 (Bakta 1.12.1 refuses older ones) directories.blast_db NCBI core_nt (or nt_prok, named in parameters.nt_version), plus the taxonomy files — directories.eggnog_db eggNOG diamond database v5.0.2 (fixed by the eggnog-mapper pin) directories.gtdbtk_db GTDB R232 (GTDB-Tk 2.7.2 pins itself to one release) directories.platon_db Platon v1.5.0 (versioned separately from Platon 1.8)

Everything else — PhiX, CARD, CheckV, dbCAN, VirSorter2, antiSMASH — is downloaded by the workflow into output_dir on the first run. All of those but PhiX also have an optional directories.*_db key: point it at a copy you already hold and nothing is fetched. Download recipes, sizes and the six optional keys are on reference databases.

docs.title: Step 3 — the keys that decide a run
docs.text:
Your copy of config/config.yaml is long, but almost all of it is tuning that can stay as shipped. These are the keys an Illumina run cannot start without:

mode: illumina

input:
  illumina_dir: /data/reads/illumina        # {sample}_R1.<ext> + {sample}_R2.<ext>

directories:
  output_dir: /data/results/run1            # everything is written here
  bakta_db:   /data/db/bakta/db
  blast_db:   /data/db/NCBI_core_nt
  eggnog_db:  /data/db/eggnog
  gtdbtk_db:  /data/db/release232
  platon_db:  /data/db/platon/db

links:
  phix_link:  https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCF/000/819/615/GCF_000819615.1_ViralProj14015/GCF_000819615.1_ViralProj14015_genomic.fna.gz
  card_link:  https://card.mcmaster.ca/download/0/broadstreet-v4.0.1.tar.bz2
  dbcan_link: https://zenodo.org/records/18622157/files/dbcan_db_v5.1.2.tar.gz

resources:
  threads: 16
  ram_gb:  64

dbcan_link already carries that value in the shipped config; phix_link and card_link are empty and required in illumina and hybrid mode — they feed the PhiX removal step and the read-based CARD screen, neither of which exists in the other two modes. Every key, with its default and what it trades off, is in configuration.

Input files are found by pattern, not listed by hand. BacFlux globs illumina_dir for {sample}_R1.<ext> files, rebuilds the R2 path per sample, and the part before _R1 becomes the sample name used in every output file:

/data/reads/illumina/
├── isolate1_R1.fastq.gz
├── isolate1_R2.fastq.gz
├── isolate2_R1.fastq.gz
└── isolate2_R2.fastq.gz         →  samples isolate1 and isolate2

All files of one kind must share one extension (fastq, fq, fastq.gz or fq.gz); mixing them stops the run. Sample names become filenames and locus tags, so fifteen characters are refused outright — * # @ % ^ / ! space ? & : ; | < > — and everything else, underscores and dots included, is accepted.

Edit a copy, not the shipped file

config/config_custom.yaml is the one name .gitignore already knows, so a copy under that name survives a git pull and never lands in a commit. Any other name runs just as well but is not ignored. Either way, leave config/config.yaml alone so you always have the commented template to read.

docs.title: Step 4 — the dry run
docs.text:
After completing database preparation and configuration, preview the jobs:

snakemake --sdm conda --configfile config/config_custom.yaml --cores 24 -n

-n (--dry-run) plans the analysis without executing jobs. It checks input discovery and the configuration conditions evaluated during planning. Inspect the header to confirm the selected mode, analysis options and samples:

… BacFlux banner …

Mode: illumina — Genomic analysis of bacterial Illumina reads.
Phage caller: virsorter2 (default). Plasmid stage: Platon-only (geNomad off).
Decontamination mode: auto (auto_vote=bp, discard_no_hit=true).
Using CheckV database from link: 'https://zenodo.org/records/21510554/files/checkv-db-v1.5.tar.gz' (db_id='checkv-db-v1.5').
Sample isolate1 will be processed.

Each of those lines is a decision you can still change: the mode, the virus caller, the decontamination policy, and every database that is being downloaded rather than read from a copy you hold. When the mobilome module is on it announces itself here too.

Compare the discovered sample list with the intended input. A mismatch can indicate a naming-pattern problem, a missing input file or an incorrect directory. Below the header, Snakemake lists the jobs. A single isolate through the default Illumina pipeline, into an empty output directory, plans 42 jobs:

Job stats:
job                                count
-------------------------------  -------
AMR_summary                            1
all                                    1
amr_contigs                            8
annotation                             1
…
trim_adapters                          1
viral_quality                          1
virsorter2_db                          1
total                                 42

The only count above one is amr_contigs: ABRicate runs once per database.

What is checked before the first job starts, and what each failure looks like:

[BacFlux] mode=illumina requires 'input.illumina_dir' to be set in the config.
[BacFlux] input.illumina_dir is not an existing directory: '/nope/reads'
[BacFlux] mode=illumina removes PhiX spike-in reads before assembly, which requires 'links.phix_link' to be set in the config.
[BacFlux] mode=illumina runs the read-based CARD AMR leg, which requires 'links.card_link' to be set in the config.
[BacFlux] directories.checkv_db points at '/data/db/checkv', which is not a directory. …
[BacFlux] Missing Illumina mate pair for sample 'isolate1': /data/reads/illumina/isolate1_R2.fastq.gz
[BacFlux] Sample name 'isolate 1' contains characters that are not allowed (' '). Rename the input files.

Each of them stops Snakemake with exit status 1, so a wrapper script or a cluster job that launched the run sees it fail.

A config with no mode at all stops with a KeyError: 'mode' from workflow/rules/shared/00_common.smk, rather than guessing a pipeline.

A wrong database path is not always caught at parse time

The five required directories.*_db paths are read but not opened while the plan is built, so a typo in one of them survives the header. Some are then caught by the dry run anyway, because they are named as rule inputs — a blast_db without the NCBI taxonomy dump beside it fails here:

MissingInputException in rule blob_json …
    affected files:
        /data/db/NCBI_core_nt/nodes.dmp
        /data/db/NCBI_core_nt/names.dmp

The rest surface when the tool itself runs. A dry run that reaches the job table means the plan is sound, not that every database is complete.

docs.title: Step 5 — the run
docs.text:
snakemake --sdm conda --configfile config/config_custom.yaml --cores 24

For local execution, --cores is the whole CPU budget and needs no other setting: every CPU-bound rule declares threads:, so --cores enforces the ceiling by itself. Do not also pass --jobs/-j: for a local run Snakemake then stops enforcing the core budget, and rules can oversubscribe the machine. See Running BacFlux for the scheduling behaviour and resource measurements.

A first run spends a long time on setup: a default Illumina run builds 21 of the 33 conda environments in workflow/envs/ and downloads the databases BacFlux fetches for itself. Environments are created under .snakemake/conda in the directory you launched from, so launching from the same place each time is what stops them being rebuilt.

The run is resumable. If it is interrupted, repeat the same command and Snakemake redoes only what is missing or out of date. After changing the configuration, inspect a new dry run to confirm which jobs Snakemake schedules for recomputation.

docs.title: What lands in the output directory
docs.text:
After a successful single-sample run, with the mobilome module off (the default):

/data/results/run1/
├── 01.reads/phix/                        # the PhiX genome and its Bowtie2 index, kept
├── 01.reads/isolate1/illumina/
│   ├── isolate1_fastp.html               # trimming report; the trimmed FASTQs are temporary
│   └── isolate1_fastp.json
├── 02.assembly/isolate1/
│   ├── contigs_final.fasta               # ← the delivered genome; every later stage reads this file
│   ├── contigs_filt.fasta                # after the length/coverage filter, before decontamination
│   ├── spades/contigs.fasta
│   ├── contaminants/
│   │   ├── contig_taxonomy_decisions.tsv # one row per contig: kept or dropped, and why
│   │   ├── isolate1_composition.txt      # genus composition of the assembly
│   │   ├── isolate1_kept_genus.txt       # the genus Bakta names the genome after
│   │   ├── isolate1_blastout
│   │   ├── contigs.list
│   │   └── bestscore.blob.blobDB.table.txt
│   └── eval/
│       ├── isolate1_qc_genomes.tsv       # which evaluated genome is which
│       └── quast/  checkm/  qualimap/
├── 03.taxonomy/isolate1/                 # GTDB-Tk classify_wf; the call is in classify/gtdbtk.*.summary.tsv
├── 04.annotation/
│   ├── bakta/isolate1/                   # the annotation: .gff3 .tsv .faa .fna .gbff
│   ├── eggnog/isolate1/
│   ├── antismash/isolate1/               # plus antismash/databases/, fetched once
│   └── dbcan/isolate1/                   # plus dbcan/dbcan_db_v5.1.2/, fetched once
├── 05.amr/
│   ├── abricate/isolate1/                # eight databases, one TSV each, plus AMR_summary.txt
│   └── mapping/isolate1/                 # the read-based CARD leg: covstats, AMR_legend, CARD_report
├── 06.plasmids/isolate1/platon/
├── 07.phages/
│   ├── virsorter/isolate1/  checkv/isolate1/
│   └── checkv_db/  vs2_db/               # fetched once and kept
├── 09.report/multiqc_report.html
└── logs/                                 # one log per job, named rule + sample

Stage numbers are the same in all four modes; a stage a mode cannot produce is simply absent (01.reads in contigs mode, 05.amr/mapping wherever there are no short reads). 08.mobilome appears only when the module is switched on — see turning it on.

Intermediates are declared temporary and deleted as soon as the last rule needing them has finished, which is why 01.reads ends up holding only reports and the PhiX genome with its index. Those two, and CARD's extracted copy under 05.amr/card_db/, are kept, so PhiX and CARD are downloaded and the PhiX index built once per output folder, and a sample added to the folder later runs without redoing the finished ones (why). Set directories.card_db to a copy you hold to skip even the CARD download.

Use these files to inspect the main results:

Question File The genome 02.assembly/{sample}/contigs_final.fasta Why was that contig kept or dropped? 02.assembly/{sample}/contaminants/contig_taxonomy_decisions.tsv Completeness and contamination estimates 02.assembly/{sample}/eval/checkm/{sample}_checkm_stats.tsv Assembly statistics 02.assembly/{sample}/eval/quast/ What species is it? 03.taxonomy/{sample}/classify/gtdbtk.*.summary.tsv What genes does it carry? 04.annotation/bakta/{sample}/ Resistance and virulence, from the contigs 05.amr/abricate/{sample}/AMR_summary.txt Resistance, from the reads 05.amr/mapping/{sample}/{sample}_CARD_report.tsv Which contigs are plasmids? 06.plasmids/{sample}/platon/verified_plasmids.txt One QC page for the whole batch 09.report/multiqc_report.html

The full layout, stage by stage, is in output files.

docs.title: Mobilome module
docs.text:
Stage 08.mobilome combines resistance-gene calls with predicted mobile genetic elements to describe genomic context and potential mobility. It reports one row per assessed gene, together with confidence fields and an audit of the supporting evidence.

The module is disabled by default. Enable it with mobilome.run: true; see Enabling the module. Its predictions do not demonstrate transfer, phenotypic resistance or the intrinsic/acquired status of a gene.

Four terms this section uses constantly

An ICE (integrative and conjugative element) sits in the chromosome and carries its own conjugation machinery, so it can move itself into another cell. An IME (integrative mobilisable element) sits in the chromosome and carries a relaxase — the enzyme that nicks the DNA to start a transfer — but no apparatus of its own, so it needs a helper element to move. An att site is the short direct repeat left at each end of an element where it integrated; finding the pair is how an element's true edges are established.

Three more abbreviations appear throughout: IS is an insertion sequence, the smallest mobile element, carrying only the genes it needs to move itself; CDS is a coding sequence, the stretch of DNA that codes for one protein; and EFSA is the European Food Safety Authority.

docs.title: Why genomic context matters
docs.text:
A gene-presence result identifies sequence evidence for a determinant. It does not establish resistance phenotype or transfer potential. A chromosomal efflux pump carried by every member of a species and a blaCTX-M gene on a conjugative plasmid give the same kind of line in an ABRicate table; only the second sits on an element that can transfer to another cell. Strain assessment asks exactly this: whether a resistance gene is intrinsic or acquired. Context informs that judgement but does not, by itself, establish intrinsic or acquired resistance.

The module supplies supporting genomic evidence for the judgement, not the judgement itself. The mobility ladder explains the six categories, the EFSA definitions behind them, their decision order and interpretation limits.

docs.title: The mobility ladder
docs.text:
Every assessed gene gets exactly one tier. The label is written into the output table next to the number, so nobody reading the TSV has to look a tier up.

Tier mobility_tier_label Context 1 intrinsic_candidate chromosomal, nothing mobile nearby 2 expression_modulation_not_mobilisation an IS upstream, on the gene's strand — expression, not mobilisation 3 composite_mobilisable_within_cell between two IS copies of one family: a composite transposon 4 named_element_mobilisable inside a curated unit transposon or integron cassette 5 mobilisable_needs_helper on a plasmid, or inside an IME 6 predicted_self_transmissible inside an ICE, or on a conjugative plasmid

Tier 5 covers every plasmid that Platon did not type conjugative, so on the plasmid route it records plasmid context rather than demonstrated helper-dependent transfer. mobility_tier_label and plasmid_mobility separate the cases: an IME and a plasmid typed mobilisable (a relaxase or oriT hit) keep mobilisable_needs_helper; a plasmid typed non_mobilisable is labelled on_plasmid_typed_non_mobilisable; a plasmid without mobility typing (unknown, for example one called by geNomad alone) keeps the generic label at medium confidence, with the audit reason plasmid_mobility_untyped.

The tiers are tested top down and the first match wins, so a curated transposon on a plasmid scores 5 or 6 rather than 4. That order, the three distance windows behind it, and how far to trust each tier — tier 4 is measured on two genomes, tier 5's IME route on none — are all on The mobility ladder.

docs.title: What runs when you turn it on
docs.text:
The module adds 22 Snakemake rules, of which 10 run on the default configuration. The other 12 belong to four optional layers, each of which stays off until you give it a source (Optional layers).

---
config:
  themeVariables:
    fontSize: 14px
  flowchart:
    nodeSpacing: 35
    rankSpacing: 25
---
flowchart LR
    C([contigs_final.fasta<br/>02.assembly])
    FAA([Bakta annotation<br/>04.annotation])
    TAX([GTDB-Tk call<br/>03.taxonomy])
    PLA([Platon calls<br/>06.plasmids])

    CL[contig_lengths]
    IS[isescan<br/>IS elements]
    IST[isescan_table]
    AFP[amrfinderplus]
    ORG[amrfinder_organism<br/>picks the organism]
    CJ[conjscan<br/>conjugation genes]
    CJI[conjscan_ice<br/>ICE and IME calls]
    REP[mobilome_replicons]

    C --> CL
    C --> IS --> IST
    FAA --> IST
    FAA --> AFP
    FAA --> CJ --> CJI
    TAX --> ORG --> AFP
    PLA --> REP

    CO[amr_mge_colocalisation<br/>sample_amr_mobility.tsv<br/>and its _audit.tsv]
    CL --> CO
    IST --> CO
    AFP --> CO
    CJI --> CO
    REP --> CO

Three things follow from that picture:

  • Two new tools, both from bioconda: ISEScan v1.7.3 for insertion sequences, and MacSyFinder v2.1.6 running the CONJscan models for conjugation machinery. Both are given up to 8 threads per sample.
  • No new database path to configure. AMRFinderPlus is already installed by Bakta and reads its database from {bakta_db}/amrfinderplus-db/latest; the CONJscan models are fetched at run time, so the machine needs network access on the first run.
  • Stage 08 consumes earlier stages rather than repeating them. It reads the assembly, the Bakta proteins, GFF3 and annotation table, the GTDB-Tk species call, and Platon's replicon calls from 06.plasmids.

The ICE/IME caller, the composite-transposon test and the att-site search run in all four modes, including illumina. The one analysis that is mode-restricted is the optional ISOSDB copy-number layer, which maps reads and therefore needs them — illumina and hybrid only.

The deliverable is one row per AMR gene in {sample}_amr_mobility.tsv, with an audit file beside it giving a reason for every gene left without context, every candidate structure rejected and every confidence cap applied. Column by column: Reading the output.

docs.title: Why the mobilome spans three stages
docs.text:
Plasmids and prophages are mobile genetic elements too, so the output layout can read as if 08.mobilome/ were "the mobilome" and 06.plasmids/ and 07.phages/ were something else. They are not. The split is by what question is being asked, not by whether the element is mobile.

Stage Question Runs 06.plasmids, 07.phages what replicons and prophages are in this genome? (detection) always 08.mobilome is each AMR gene in a mobile element, and how transferable? (interpretation), plus IS, transposon, integron and ICE detection opt-in

For the detection stages, see Plasmids and Prophages.

docs.title: Why it is off by default
docs.text:
Scope. Enable the module when the analysis requires genomic context and predicted mobility in addition to gene detection. The always-on AMR analyses — ABRicate on the contigs, and the CARD read screen in the modes that have short reads — are unaffected by this switch (Antimicrobial resistance).

Cost. Ten extra rules on the default path, three of them per-sample tool runs at up to 8 threads, plus a one-off model download.

Before you switch it on. Turning the module on fetches the CONJscan model package, which Institut Pasteur / CNRS license under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. BacFlux never ships it — you download it, under your own agreement with the licensor, exactly as with bakta_db and the other user-supplied databases. Licence types for every tool, model set and database are listed on Licensing.

docs.title: Three things to know before reading the output
docs.text:
1. On a fragmented assembly a located IS count is a lower bound. IS elements are a leading cause of contig breaks: identical copies collapse in the assembly graph, so the assembler cannot tell which flank belongs to which copy and breaks there. The AMR gene and its flanking IS regularly land on different contigs. Every row therefore carries dist_to_contig_end, is_at_contig_boundary and spans_contigs, and the IS summary reports what fraction of IS calls sit within 100 bp of a contig end (mobilome.contig_boundary_bp). Read those before reading the counts.

2. Never write "transmissible". Tier 6 is predicted_self_transmissible, and the prediction rests on finding conjugation machinery, not on watching a transfer happen.

3. Confidence is tiered, never a bare call. IS calling is imperfect even on manually curated genomes: benchmarking four tools against a curated E. coli annotation, Puterová & Martínek (2021) put the "improbable or not an IS element" discovery rate between 0% and 23.7% depending on the tool, with ISEScan — the caller BacFlux uses — at 8.0% (2.2% on their larger ISbrowser set). So every row carries confidence (high / medium / low), and anything resting on a contig boundary or on a partial hit is capped at low. Two predictable false calls are also removed before anything reads the IS table: False IS21 calls over replication genes explains them.

The module was validated on closed genomes and then measured again on deliberately fragmented ones — 40 benchmark genomes cut to ~150 kb, ~50 kb and ~20 kb N50, re-annotated and re-run end to end:

closed 150 kb N50 50 kb N50 20 kb N50 curated ICEs detected (of 18) 15 15 15 12 median called ÷ true element length 0.55 0.45 0.34 0.22 ICE/IME calls at confidence: high 24% 19% 10% 3%

On this benchmark the class of an element survived fragmentation better than its extent. A low-confidence call on a draft means the assembly could not support a stronger claim, not that the call is wrong. Which columns to read and what not to conclude: Draft assemblies.

docs.title: False IS21 calls over replication genes
docs.text:
The problem. ISEScan finds insertion sequences (IS) by looking for the proteins they carry. One IS family, IS21, carries two: a transposase, IstA, and a helper protein, IstB. IstB belongs to the same protein family as two of the cell's own DNA-replication proteins (Koonin 1992; Arias-Palomo & Berger 2015):

  • DnaA, which starts chromosome replication;
  • the replicative helicase loader: DnaC in E. coli, Salmonella, Klebsiella and their close relatives, and DnaI in Bacillus, Listeria, Staphylococcus, Streptococcus and other Bacilli.

Because they look alike, two of ISEScan's IS21 models also match these genes, and ISEScan reports "a partial IS21 element" sitting on top of them. Puterová & Martínek (2021) found the same hits over dnaA, dnaC and dnaI, and Nakajima et al. (2026) removed ISEScan calls over dnaA as artefacts. The calls are false: these genes are essential (Kobayashi et al. 2003; Baba et al. 2006), so an insertion inside one would not leave a living isolate. Left in, each call adds one IS to the counts, and it could make a resistance gene nearby look as if it sat beside a mobile element. In BacFlux's own runs the call over dnaA appeared in all 16 genomes checked, and the call over the helicase loader in about half of the benchmark genomes.

For dnaA, the gene's name is enough. A call lying over a gene Bakta names dnaA goes to {sample}_is_discarded.tsv with the reason overlaps_dnaA. On the 16 genomes checked, this removed exactly one call per genome, the false one, and nothing else. The call often runs on into the next genes, dnaN and recF. It is still removed, because the test asks whether the call and the gene share at least half of whichever is shorter: a call that holds all of dnaA counts even when most of it lies outside.

For dnaC and dnaI, the name is not enough. Bakta also gives those names to look-alike genes that really are on mobile elements: the helicase loaders of prophages, such as Gifsy-1 and Gifsy-2 in Salmonella LT2 (Słomiński et al. 2007), loaders carried by ICEs, and even the IstB of a real IS21 element. In E. coli and its relatives, every DnaC-type gene other than the chromosome's own sits inside a phage, transposon or IS21 element (Brézellec et al. 2016). Removing every call over a gene named dnaC or dnaI would have deleted 15 real calls in BacFlux's test data.

Filtering criterion: conserved neighbouring genes. The chromosome's own loader sits next to a fixed partner gene:

  • dnaC shares an operon with dnaT (Masai & Arai 1988);
  • dnaI shares one with dnaB, and nrdR is the next gene along, 1–3 kb from dnaI (Bruand & Ehrlich 1995; Elfmann et al. 2025).

Phage and ICE loaders do not have that neighbour: in BacFlux's test data the nearest one was over 100 kb away. So a call is removed, with the reason overlaps_helicase_loader, only when all of these hold:

  • ISEScan calls it a partial IS21 element;
  • the call and a gene Bakta names dnaC or dnaI share at least half of whichever is shorter;
  • that gene's partner lies within 5 kb of it;
  • no IS21 transposase (istA) lies within 5 kb, which would mean a real IS21 element.

Tuning gives the exact test and where its settings live.

Examples

Genome Call over Partner nearby? Result E. coli K-12, K. pneumoniae dnaC dnaT, right beside it removed: a false call B. subtilis 168 dnaI nrdR, 1.6 kb away removed: a false call Salmonella LT2 its own dnaC dnaT, right beside it removed: a false call Salmonella LT2, Gifsy-1 and Gifsy-2 prophages the phage's own loader, named dnaC no kept: it is on a mobile element Shigella flexneri virulence plasmid the IstB of an IS21, named dnaC no; istA 1.5 kb away kept: a real IS21 element Paenibacillus dnaI no nrdR nearby; the genus has another gene order kept: the partner cannot be checked

What this rests on. The protein family, the false hits and the gene order are published (see the references below). The partner test, its 5 kb windows and the figures that follow are BacFlux's own, measured on 176 datasets: 52 public benchmark genomes plus validation and test runs. There, the rule removed 59 calls, all of them false. It kept every one of the 57 real IS21 elements and every phage, ICE and plasmid loader, and it changed no ICE call, mobility tier or confidence. About 16 false calls stay, in taxa where the partner gene is absent, such as Paenibacillus, Clostridioides and Aquifex, or where a fragmented draft put it on another contig. They stay in the IS table, as they would without the rule.

docs.title: Draft assemblies
docs.text:
Fragmentation affects both mobile-element detection and boundary recovery. This page reports a simulated-fragmentation benchmark and explains which output fields to inspect on a draft assembly.

Read mge_class and confidence with spans_contigs and at_contig_boundary. Inspect boundary_method before interpreting coordinates or element length. The benchmark is informative about the tested assemblies; its N50 bands are not universal acceptance criteria.

Terms used on this page

AMR antimicrobial resistance IS insertion sequence — the smallest mobile element, carrying only the genes it needs to move itself ICE integrative and conjugative element — carries its own conjugation machinery, so it can move itself into another cell IME integrative mobilisable element — carries a relaxase but no apparatus of its own, so it needs a helper element AICE actinomycete integrative and conjugative element MPF mating pair formation — the apparatus that builds the bridge between two cells att site the short direct repeat left at each end of an element where it integrated

docs.title: How this was measured
docs.text:
40 benchmark genomes — 28 carrying 30 curated ICE or IME elements, and 12 negative controls — were cut into contigs at three contiguities, re-annotated with Bakta and re-run through the whole chain with the same commands and parameters as the closed runs. 120 assemblies, 191 draft calls.

The closed and the draft runs both had the optional ICEscan model set switched on. It is off by default. Without it fewer IMEs are found: with the current code, 2 of the 12 on the closed genomes instead of 5 (Validation). On a default run, expect fewer IMEs than the tables below show.

Arm Target N50 Achieved (median) Contigs (median) Curated elements still on one contig good 150 kb 135 kb 32 21/30 typical 50 kb 48 kb 82 14/30 poor 20 kb 20 kb 180 8/30

Breaks were placed at IS elements first, then rRNA operons, then at random — because that is what breaks a real assembly — and sequence was deleted at each break. Contigs were length-sorted and about half reverse-complemented, so cross-contig clustering could not be flattered by contigs happening to sit in genome order.

To see which arm matches your data, compare your assembly's N50 in the QUAST report (02.assembly/{sample}/eval/quast/) with the table above. A failure at "good" is a serious result; a failure at "poor" may simply be the assembly.

docs.title: What degrades, and by how much
docs.text:
closed good (150 kb) typical (50 kb) poor (20 kb) ICE detected (of 18 curated) 15 15 15 12 IME detected (of 12 curated) 5 4 3 3 median called ÷ true length 0.55 0.45 0.34 0.22 median called ÷ largest surviving piece 0.55 0.57 0.77 0.72 median call precision (overlap ÷ call length) 1.0 1.0 1.0 1.0 spans_contigs = TRUE 0 13 27 32 at_contig_boundary = TRUE 3 7 21 23 confidence high 24% 19% 10% 3% confidence low 10% 34% 63% 65% boundary_method = none 44% 77% 82% 90% calls on the 12 negative controls 5 4 3 2

Three things there matter more than the rest.

Detection is flat down to 50 kb N50. ICE recall is identical to the closed genomes at both 150 kb and 50 kb, and only breaks at 20 kb. The IME arm is weak everywhere, closed genomes included. Most IMEs missed on the drafts were already missed on the closed genomes, among them the three smallest (522 bp, 1.2 kb and 5.1 kb). So fragmentation costs 2 IMEs, not 9.

The length collapses, but the caller is not what lost it. Against the true element the median recovered length falls from 0.55 to 0.22. Against the largest surviving contig piece — the ceiling any per-contig caller can reach — it is 0.55 → 0.57 → 0.77 → 0.72, flat or better. The caller keeps recovering the same share of what is still visible. The missing bases are the assembly's.

Checks within the simulated benchmark. Across the 191 reported draft calls: no fabricated att sequence (every pair reported on a draft occurs at least twice in the corresponding closed genome), no class promoted at high confidence, no new false positive on a negative control, and not one violation of the caller's own confidence rules in 163 checks.

docs.title: Where the line is
docs.text:
Not between "good" and "poor" — between classification and extent.

N50 What to do with the calls ≥ 150 kb in this benchmark, ICE detection matched the closed runs; still inspect boundaries and individual evidence ≈ 50 kb class detection remained relatively robust in this benchmark (ICE 15/18, and 91% of calls land on some curated entry for these accessions). The extent is not: median 0.34× the true length, 82% of calls with boundary_method=none. Read the class, ignore the length ≈ 20 kb detection itself starts to go (12/18), 65% of calls are low confidence, and 59% of MacSyFinder's systems join genes from different contigs. Not wrong, but no longer informative

Each sample's own contig count and N50 are written as the first row of its {sample}_ice_discarded.tsv (action = assembly_qc), with one sentence saying which band it falls in. Read that before the calls.

docs.title: Which columns to read
docs.text:
These are the columns of {sample}_ice_candidates.tsv, the element table. The AMR table beside it repeats the two contig flags under slightly different names — is_at_contig_boundary for at_contig_boundary, and spans_contigs unchanged — so check the header of whichever file you have open (head -1 file | tr '\t' '\n' | nl).

These fields support interpretation of the available evidence:

Column Why mge_class ICE / IME / AICE / passive island / conjugative region. Class may change or be lost as evidence is fragmented; no high-confidence promotion was observed in this sweep mobility the sentence that goes with the class. Always "predicted self-transmissible" confidence every high call in the benchmark satisfied the documented rule and was corroborated by the closed genome spans_contigs TRUE = the evidence is on more than one contig. Absolute cap at low — 72 TRUE calls in the sweep, 72 at low, no exceptions at_contig_boundary TRUE = the element runs into a contig end. Also an absolute cap: 54 TRUE, 54 at low boundary_method read before any coordinate. tRNA = ends taken from a tRNA-anchored att pair and applied to start/end; denovo = a lead, never acted on; none = the interval is the machinery span only machinery_intact, n_anchor_classes what the class actually rests on mpf_from_other_contig TRUE = this is an ICE only because the mating-pair genes are on a different contig

Treat as a floor, never a measurement, whenever boundary_method = none: start, end, length_bp. At the typical arm, calls on elements fragmentation had genuinely broken reported a median 19% of the element.

Do not do on a draft: compare element lengths between samples, or do arithmetic on length_bp — total mobilome burden, percent of genome mobile, and so on. Those numbers are governed by your assembly, not by the biology.

docs.title: What a low-confidence call means
docs.text:
Low confidence records limitations in the supporting evidence. It does not establish that a call is correct or incorrect. Confidence is set by the guards above, and on a fragmented assembly those conditions are the normal state of affairs, which is why low-confidence calls go from 10% on closed genomes to 63% at 50 kb N50.

Evidence that the low tier is not simply noise: on the 12 negative controls the number of calls went down under fragmentation (5 → 4 → 3 → 2), none at high confidence, and not one at a locus the closed genome had not already called. Contig ends did not manufacture false positives; they removed evidence.

So a low-confidence call on a draft is a lead worth following — look at spans_contigs, the missing components and the audit file to see what was lost — not a result to report, and not one to discard silently.

docs.title: The direction that stays safe, and the one exemption
docs.text:
Per call, back-translated onto the closed genome's coordinates:

good typical poor demoted vs the closed call 8 26 34 … ICE → IME (tra operon lost) 1 5 5 … ICE → conjugative region (integrase lost) 7 16 20 promoted vs the closed call 0 1 0 … at high confidence 0 0 0 calls created where the closed genome had nothing 1 1 1 … at high confidence 0 0 0

The dangerous direction is essentially empty, and the single promotion carries spans_contigs=TRUE and low confidence — the guard caught it. Total ICE-class calls fall 37 → 32 → 24 → 16: fragmentation makes the module more conservative about tier 6, not less.

mpf_from_other_contig = TRUE — the row that reads as self-contradictory

On a draft the tra operon routinely lands on a different contig from the relaxase, so a cluster with no mating-pair gene of its own is still called an ICE when the typed system's other hits are elsewhere. Without that exemption real ICEs get demoted the moment an assembly breaks. The cost is a row saying mobility = predicted self-transmissible next to missing_components = mating-pair apparatus.

The flag fired on 9 of 191 draft calls and on 0 of 68 closed-genome calls. All 9 also carry spans_contigs = TRUE, so all 9 are already at low confidence. Read such a row as conjugation machinery is present in this genome and may belong to this element — the evidence for the mating bridge is not on the contig you are looking at, and cannot be checked there.

One thing MacSyFinder cannot see. It runs with --db-type ordered_replicon, so on a draft it treats the whole assembly as one replicon. At the good, typical and poor arms, 28%, 50% and 59% of its systems spanned more than one contig. In 87–93% of those, the joined genes were not next to each other in the real genome. At good the median gap between them was 1.36 Mb. BacFlux's own caller clusters per contig, so no reported interval joins sequence from two contigs. The damage is limited to the system type a call inherits from MacSyFinder. The spans_contigs and mpf_from_other_contig columns flag it.

docs.title: One worked call, closed and broken
docs.text:
ICEMsp.M1D, a 199,376 bp chromosomal ICE in a Mesorhizobium sp. (CP034444.1). Values taken verbatim from {sample}_ice_candidates.tsv in each run.

closed good typical poor element on how many contigs 1 3 9 13 largest surviving piece 100% 79% 60% 14% mge_class ice conjugative_region conjugative_region conjugative_region length_bp 39,437 16,002 16,002 13,132 has_integrase TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE boundary_method denovo none none none spans_contigs FALSE FALSE FALSE TRUE confidence high high high low

The class demotes for a stated reason: the integrase is lost to a contig break, and without one the caller refuses to say "ICE". It does not guess.

Look at the good column. That call is high confidence with both warning flags FALSE, and both flags are literally true — the machinery cluster is entirely on one contig, well away from its ends — while the element continues on contigs the caller never looked at. confidence answers is this conjugation machinery, and of what class. It does not answer does this interval delimit the element. boundary_method is the only column that answers the second question, which is why it has to be read first. This is not a one-off: at good, 5 of the 7 detected-but-broken elements carry no warning flag at all while reporting a median 19% of the element.

What to conclude from that row: this genome carries conjugation machinery of MPF type T on one contig, with a relaxase and an intact apparatus, and the region is a real finding worth following up. What not to conclude: that the element is 16 kb; that it is not an ICE (the integrase is elsewhere in the assembly, not absent from the genome); or that the 16 kb interval defines its cargo.

docs.title: Two guards added after this measurement
docs.text:
The sweep exposed two gaps, and a guard was added for each. Neither changes anything on a closed genome: re-run with both guards in place, the 68 closed-genome calls came back with no difference in any column. On the 120 fragmented assemblies the only changes were the new flag and the ten boundary claims withdrawn below; every class, confidence and coordinate stayed the same.

1. A de novo repeat is now counted across the whole assembly, not just its contig. A de novo search requires exactly two matching copies as an operational specificity rule, so the att search already refused a repeat with three or more. But it counted the copies on the contig it was given. On a closed genome each contig is a whole replicon, so the two counts rarely differ. On a draft they often do. All 35 de novo repeats reported on the drafts had exactly two copies on their own contig, but 10 of them had 3 to 30 copies across the assembly — repeat families, not integration scars. The worst, an 89 bp repeat with 30 copies, was attached to a high-confidence call. Those ten boundary claims are now withdrawn: the att columns are cleared, boundary_method goes back to none, and {sample}_ice_discarded.tsv records the reason denovo_att_is_a_repeat_family. No coordinate moves, because a de novo repeat never widened an element in the first place.

The assembly-wide count is not yet applied to tRNA-anchored pairs: their copies are still counted on their own contig only. That matters, because a tRNA-anchored pair is the kind that moves an element's edges, and so decides which AMR genes count as cargo. The gap is left open on purpose for now. A tRNA-anchored pair is a stronger claim to begin with, since one copy has to overlap an annotated tRNA. Extending the count to it would change calls and could lose real elements, so it needs its own benchmark run first.

2. A new column marks an ICE whose mating-pair genes are on another contig. This is mpf_from_other_contig, described in the warning box above, and it is for information only. It changes no class: the row stays an ICE, so a real ICE is not demoted just because a contig break moved its mating-pair genes onto another contig. It changes no confidence, because spans_contigs already caps these rows at low.

A guard that was considered and rejected on the evidence. Refusing to widen an element onto an att pair when either copy sits near a contig end sounds prudent, but it would have done harm. Four tRNA-anchored pairs on the drafts sat within 2 kb of a contig end. Three of them give exactly the same element length as the closed genome. The fourth is the ICEEc2 positive control (GU725392), recovered at 99.9% precision; its pair sits 26 bp from the end of the closed record too, because the deposited record is the element. The guard would have cost a positive control and caught nothing: every one of the 43 att pairs reported on the drafts is sequence that occurs at least twice in the closed genome. It was not added.

docs.title: What this measurement could not establish
docs.text:
These are simulated breaks, not real short-read assemblies.

  • The cuts are cleaner than an assembler's. Repeat-driven breakpoints are 68% of all breaks at the good arm but only 33% at typical and 14% at poor — the genomes simply do not contain enough IS and rRNA to reach 20 kb N50 — so the two harsher arms cut closer to uniform than reality, which under-breaks elements and makes those arms optimistic.
  • No misassemblies. A real draft contains contigs that chimerically join non-contiguous sequence within one contig. That is exactly what per-contig clustering cannot see, and nothing here tests it.
  • No read-level effects — coverage variation, collapsed repeats and the IS copy-number collapse are not represented at all. The optional ISOSDB layer is what puts a number on the last of those.

The IME arm is underpowered (3–5 of 12) and the negative-control arm is small (2–5 calls), so those rows carry wide uncertainty. And several of ICEberg's own element boundaries are themselves predictions, so "agrees with the curated length" means agreement with a curation, not with truth.

docs.title: Enabling the mobilome module
docs.text:
mobilome:
  run: true

Set mobilome.run: true in the configuration used for the run. The core module reuses the configured Bakta database and downloads CONJscan models as needed, so it requires no additional database path. Optional layers have separate sources.

Everything else in the mobilome: block is either a threshold with a sensible default or one of the four optional layers, each of which stays off until you give it a source of its own (Optional layers).

Terms used on this page

AMR antimicrobial resistance IS insertion sequence — the smallest mobile element, carrying only the genes it needs to move itself ICE integrative and conjugative element — sits in the chromosome and carries its own conjugation machinery IME integrative mobilisable element — sits in the chromosome but needs a helper element to move att site the short direct repeat left at each end of an element where it integrated HMM hidden Markov model — a statistical profile of a gene or protein family

docs.title: What run: true adds
docs.text:
Ten rules on the default configuration, of which three are per-sample tool runs at up to 8 threads.

Added What it does AMRFinderPlus the AMR calls the module reasons about, with coordinates, a Method column and a partial-at-contig-end flag ISEScan 1.7.3 insertion sequences on the delivered genome MacSyFinder 2.1.6 running the CONJscan models relaxase, coupling protein and mating-pair apparatus — the machinery behind an ICE, an IME or a conjugative plasmid four helper steps replicon calls from Platon, contig lengths, the ICE/IME caller with its att-site search, and the co-localisation that writes the deliverable

Two of those are new conda environments, both from bioconda. AMRFinderPlus is not new: it is already installed by Bakta, and reads its database from {bakta_db}/amrfinderplus-db/latest — so that AMRFinderPlus data do not need a separate download. CONJscan models are obtained separately on first use.

Stage 08 consumes earlier stages rather than repeating them. It reads the delivered genome, the Bakta proteins, GFF3 and annotation table, the GTDB-Tk species call, and Platon's replicon calls from 06.plasmids. Nothing in it re-detects a plasmid or a prophage.

The first run needs network access

The CONJscan model package is fetched at run time by msf_data install. It is a versioned package, so unlike the optional layers it needs no PROVENANCE.txt — the version is already recoverable. The rule writes the models' licence notice to the top of its own log.

docs.title: What runs in which mode
docs.text:
The ICE/IME caller, the composite-transposon test and the att-site search run in all four modes, illumina included. The constraint on them is assembly contiguity, not the sequencer — and every call carries the flags that say how contiguous the assembly under it was (Draft assemblies).

The one mode-restricted analysis is the optional ISOSDB copy-number layer, which maps reads and therefore needs them: illumina and hybrid only.

docs.title: --organism, and why the taxonomy stage matters here
docs.text:
AMRFinderPlus checks curated point mutations when a supported organism is selected. This supplements gene-presence screening, which does not resolve the specific substitutions from a presence call alone. A mutation result does not itself establish intrinsic resistance or lack of transfer potential; see The mobility ladder.

So the module maps the GTDB-Tk call onto an AMRFinderPlus organism name and passes --organism when a confident mapping exists. There is no official convention for that translation — GTDB's own FAQ states there is no direct mapping to NCBI taxa — so BacFlux uses project-local, release-specific mapping tables and curated refusal rules. The mapping is documented and audited; it is not an authoritative reconciliation of the two taxonomies:

  • every decision, including every refusal, is written to {sample}_amrfinder_organism_audit.tsv with its reason;
  • a genome with no confident mapping gets no --organism rather than a guess;
  • without --organism, {sample}_amrfinderplus_mutations.tsv holds a single line stating that point-mutation screening was not available: not assessed, never none found.

Re-check the table when you change the GTDB release.

The other AMR analyses are untouched

ABRicate and the CARD read screen keep running exactly as before. The three analyses are complementary: the CARD read screen detects genes the assembly collapsed or broke, ABRicate screens eight databases, and AMRFinderPlus supplies the structured gene and mutation output this module uses. See Antimicrobial resistance.

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text:
Time. Three extra tool runs per sample, each capped at 8 threads, plus a one-off model download. On a typical bacterial isolate none of them is close to eggNOG or GTDB-Tk in cost.

Disk. The model package and the per-sample isescan/ and conjscan/ trees, kept as raw evidence.

A licence decision. Turning the module on fetches the CONJscan models, which Institut Pasteur / CNRS license under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. BacFlux never ships them — you download them, under your own agreement with the licensor, exactly as with bakta_db. Selecting the module prints the notice at parse time. Licence types for everything the module can fetch are on Licensing.

docs.title: The rest of the block
docs.text:
mobilome:
  run: false
  max_composite_span_bp: 20000       # two IS copies further apart are not one composite
  coverage_profile: 0.5              # how much of an HMM profile a hit must cover
  contig_boundary_bp: 100            # how close to a contig end counts as "at the edge"
  require_trna_boundary_for_high: false
  icescan:   { run: false, ... }     # ─┐ the four optional layers, all off by
  tncentral: { url: "", ... }        #  │ default: ICEscan by its own run flag,
  iceberg:   { urls: [], ... }       #  │ the other three because they have
  isosdb:    { fasta_url: "", ... }  # ─┘ nowhere yet to fetch from

ICEscan is the only one of the four that ships a working URL, because it has a single canonical source — the bundle EBI publishes for ICEfinder2 — so run: true is all it needs. For the other three you paste a URL in yourself, and the commented # e.g. line beside each key is the address that was used to validate this module. Each of the four also takes a local dir instead, and iceberg.dir accepts the iceberg_db folder an earlier BacFlux run built.

Two of them need explaining before a first run.

  • coverage_profile (default 0.5, MacSyFinder's own default) is the fraction of a profile HMM an alignment must cover before the hit is kept. It is not identity and not an E-value: a hit can be statistically beyond doubt and still be dropped by this rule alone. Every validated result in these docs was measured at 0.5. What lowering it buys and costs, over all three benchmark sets, is on Tuning.
  • require_trna_boundary_for_high (default false) demands a tRNA-anchored att site before any element may be called high confidence. Sensible on closed long-read assemblies, where an unresolved boundary is a warning sign; on a draft it is the norm, which is why it is off by default.

Every key, in the file's own order, is in Configuration.

docs.title: Confirming it is on
docs.text:
The parse-time header names the module before any job starts, alongside the mode and the phage caller. If it is not in the header, it is not running — check that you edited the config you passed on the command line.

Output lands in 08.mobilome/: one directory per sample, plus the shared model and database directories at the top of the stage. See Reading the output.

docs.title: The mobility ladder
docs.text:
The module assigns a numbered tier to each assessable gene using the detected element and replicon context. The output includes both the tier and its label. The categories summarise the evidence selected by the decision rules; they are not measurements of transfer rate or probabilities of resistance spread. Genes without usable coordinates are reported as not_assessable.

The five terms the table uses

An IS (insertion sequence) is the smallest mobile element: it encodes only what it needs to move itself and carries no passenger genes, so an IS can never be the resistance gene — only its neighbour.

A composite transposon is what you get when two copies of the same IS land either side of something: the whole block, cargo included, can then move as a unit.

An integron is a capture system with a cassette array; a resistance gene sitting in a cassette has an architecture somebody has characterised and named.

An ICE (integrative and conjugative element) sits in the chromosome and carries its own conjugation machinery, so it can move itself into another cell.

An IME (integrative mobilisable element) also sits in the chromosome and carries a relaxase — the enzyme that nicks the DNA to start a transfer — but no apparatus of its own, so it needs a helper element to move.

That last distinction is the whole difference between tier 5 and tier 6.

Two abbreviations used throughout: AMR is antimicrobial resistance, and EFSA is the European Food Safety Authority.

Tier mobility_tier_label Context What it means 1 intrinsic_candidate chromosomal, nothing mobile nearby no stronger mobile context was assigned by the enabled methods 2 expression_modulation_not_mobilisation an IS sits upstream, on the gene's strand an upstream IS can be consistent with promoter-mediated expression changes; this context alone does not establish gene mobilisation 3 composite_mobilisable_within_cell the gene sits between two copies of the same IS family a pattern consistent with a candidate composite transposon; activity is not experimentally established 4 named_element_mobilisable the gene sits inside a curated unit transposon or integron cassette mobilisable, with an architecture somebody has characterised and named 5 mobilisable_needs_helper on a plasmid, or inside an IME an IME, or a plasmid typed mobilisable, can transfer only with a helper element; for other plasmids see the note below 6 predicted_self_transmissible inside an ICE, or on a conjugative plasmid predicted self-transmissible

Tier 5 covers every plasmid that Platon did not type conjugative, so on the plasmid route it records plasmid context rather than demonstrated helper-dependent transfer. mobility_tier_label and plasmid_mobility separate the cases: an IME and a plasmid typed mobilisable (a relaxase or oriT hit) keep mobilisable_needs_helper; a plasmid typed non_mobilisable is labelled on_plasmid_typed_non_mobilisable; a plasmid without mobility typing (unknown, for example one called by geNomad alone) keeps the generic label at medium confidence, with the audit reason plasmid_mobility_untyped.

docs.title: How one tier is chosen
docs.text:
The tiers are tested from the top down, and the first match wins. The order is written out here exactly as the code applies it:

  1. inside an ICE → 6
  2. on a plasmid Platon typed conjugative → 6
  3. inside an IME → 5
  4. on any other plasmid → 5
  5. inside a curated named element → 4
  6. between two IS copies of one family → 3
  7. an IS within 500 bp upstream, same strand → 2
  8. none of the above → 1

Two consequences follow. A more specific call beats a broader one: an ICE (an interval) is preferred over a conjugative plasmid (a whole replicon) when both would give tier 6, and the winning element is named in mge_id. And a curated transposon on a plasmid scores 5 or 6, not 4, because the replicon evidence is tested first — which is why tier 4 is reached only when a curated name is the strongest thing available, in practice on the chromosome.

Evidence for a lower tier is kept when a higher tier is assigned: it goes to the audit file (named_element_overrides_composite_pattern, inside_named_element_but_higher_tier_applies and others), and a curated transposon or integron containing the gene stays in named_element and named_element_type. mge_name names the element that set the tier.

docs.title: The three windows that define the tiers
docs.text:
None of them is a biological constant. Every row therefore reports the measured distance next to the tier, so a reader who disagrees with a threshold can re-judge the row without re-running anything.

Window Value Used for upstream promoter distance 500 bp tier 2. ISEcp1 sits 42–266 bp upstream of blaCTX-M; beyond 500 bp an intervening gene is likely and the mechanism becomes speculative context window 5,000 bp how close any IS must be before it is reported as mge_context at all composite span 20,000 bp (mobilome.max_composite_span_bp) tier 3. Real composites run from ~2.5 kb to ~25 kb

The only one that is a config key is the composite span. See Tuning.

docs.title: Two things the ladder deliberately does not do
docs.text:
A gene with no usable coordinates is NA / not_assessable, never tier 1. "We could not assess this" and "we assessed it and found nothing" are different results, and collapsing them would turn missing data into an intrinsic-resistance claim.

An IS that has landed inside the coding sequence is reported separately. That usually inactivates the gene, so it gets its own is_inside_amr_cds flag rather than being folded into a mobility call.

docs.title: Intrinsic versus acquired — the framing this exists to serve
docs.text:
An AMR gene list records genomic detection evidence. Phenotypic resistance and transfer potential require separate interpretation. Chromosomal location, species prevalence and mobile-element context answer related but distinct questions. A chromosomal efflux pump carried by every member of a species and a blaCTX-M gene on a conjugative plasmid give the same kind of line in an ABRicate table; only the second sits on an element that can transfer to another cell.

The regulatory framing rests on the distinction between intrinsic and acquired resistance, and the definitions are explicit:

Intrinsic AMR gene — "Gene inherent to strains of a bacterial species … An AMR gene is considered 'intrinsic' when it is shared by the vast majority of wild type strains of the same species (or subspecies) and is restricted to those located on the chromosome."

Acquired AMR gene — "A resistance gene novel for the strain under assessment, acquired through horizontal transfer … Acquired AMR genes could be integrated in the bacterial chromosome or harboured on a separate genetic element."

— EFSA Scientific Committee (2025), Guidance on the characterisation of microorganisms in support of the risk assessment of products used in the food chain, Glossary. https://doi.org/10.2903/j.efsa.2025.9705

The method for deciding the intrinsic side is published separately by EFSA BIOHAZ (2023), together with a tool for the automated analysis of gene distribution across a species.

Why tier 1 says candidate

Both halves of the definition are population-level, and BacFlux implements no population comparison of any kind — every analysis is per genome. Two things follow:

  • Intrinsic cannot be established from one genome. It is a claim about the species.
  • Chromosomal does not mean intrinsic. An acquired gene may perfectly well sit on the chromosome.

So tier 1 is intrinsic_candidate: the module observed a chromosomal gene with no mobile-element context, which is consistent with intrinsic and does not establish it. The confirmatory work is a species-wide distribution analysis plus phenotypic testing.

The module produces supporting evidence for the intrinsic-versus-acquired judgement. It does not produce the judgement, it is not "EFSA-compliant" and does not claim to be. The full argument, with sources, is in methods_amr_intrinsic_acquired.md.

docs.title: The one place a single genome speaks to the intrinsic side
docs.text:
AMRFinderPlus can assess curated substitutions in genes such as gyrA, rpoB or rpsL when an appropriate organism setting is available. A mutation call alone does not establish species-wide intrinsic resistance or absence of transfer. A gene-presence summary cannot distinguish the relevant substitutions: query a susceptible genome for gyrA and you get ~99.9% identity, query a resistant one and you get ~99.9% identity, because the one residue that decides the phenotype is averaged away inside the percentage.

AMRFinderPlus with --organism asks the other question — not "is gyrA here" but "is residue 83 of GyrA a serine or a leucine" — and reports the hit with Method: POINTX or POINTP. That is why the module maps the GTDB-Tk call onto an AMRFinderPlus organism where it can, and why the mutations file is a separate deliverable (Enabling the module).

Without --organism, {sample}_amrfinderplus_mutations.tsv holds a single line stating that point-mutation screening was not available. That means not assessed, not "no mutations found": AMRFinderPlus curates point mutations for 30 mostly clinical organisms (in the AMRFinderPlus database that comes with the Bakta database), and the reason no organism was passed is written to {sample}_amrfinder_organism_audit.tsv.

docs.title: Language discipline
docs.text: Tier 6 is predicted_self_transmissible, and the qualifier is never dropped. The prediction rests on finding conjugation machinery that looks complete, not on watching a transfer happen. The confirmatory experiment is a filter or broth mating assay, and no output of this module substitutes for one.

docs.title: How far to trust a tier
docs.text:
Tiers 1, 2, 3 and 6 are the ones you will meet in practice, and they are the ones the benchmark exercises. Two tiers are rarer than their position in the table suggests.

Tier 4 is structurally uncommon, not broken. It needs three things at once: the opt-in TnCentral naming layer configured, a curated transposon or integron actually containing the gene, and the gene not on a plasmid and not inside an ICE or IME — because those are tested first and the first match wins. A resistance gene in a curated transposon on a plasmid scores tier 5, not tier 4.

Nothing is lost when that happens: the curated name is still written to named_element and named_element_type, and the audit file records inside_named_element_but_higher_tier_applies. So you can always see that a gene sat in a named element even when its tier came from somewhere else.

It is also strict about evidence: a curated element must be present at ≥80% of its reference length before it may name anything. What decides tier 4 is therefore whether the element survived assembly intact, not whether the genome is closed. On a draft where the transposon sits on a single contig it is reached readily; where assembly broke the element up, the same transposon survives only as a fragment and is refused. Worked through on a real genome, both halves of that — the override and the 80% refusal — are on Worked example.

Tier 5 has two routes, and only one is well exercised. The plasmid route — the gene is on a plasmid — is common and benchmarked. The IME route, where a chromosomal gene sits inside an integrative mobilisable element, is much rarer, and the benchmark has not put an AMR gene inside one.

What to do with that. Tier 4 has been measured on closed positive controls and has since been seen on draft assemblies too; the tier 5 IME route has not been exercised at all. Tier 4 counts need care either way: a curated element carrying a resistance cluster yields as many rows as it has genes, so a single run can report ten or fifteen tier 4 rows that are all one transposon. Read the count as elements as much as genes. For reporting, assess the evidence columns alongside the tier — named_element, mge_id, boundary_method and confidence are all there for exactly this. The measured performance of the tiers that are benchmarked is on Validation, including the boundary caveat that applies to tier 1.

One more thing to expect before reading a tier 4 count: the curated transposon catalogues are rich in mercury- and arsenic-resistance elements — the Tn21 and Tn5053 families — and AMRFinderPlus with --plus reports those as STRESS rather than AMR. A tier 4 row is quite often a metal-resistance operon and not an antibiotic one, so read amr_element_type next to the tier before concluding anything about antibiotics.

docs.text:
