|-- 09.report/                                   multiqc_report.html
`-- logs/                                        one file per rule per sample

docs.title: 01.reads — read QC and filtering
docs.text:
Absent entirely in contigs mode, which has no reads to QC.

Path Written by Contents {sample}/illumina/{sample}_fastp.html trim_adapters fastp's adapter- and quality-trimming report, for a human. {sample}/illumina/{sample}_fastp.json trim_adapters The same numbers for MultiQC. {sample}/illumina/{sample}_sel_R{1,2}.fastq map_sel_contigs [hybrid] The Illumina pairs that mapped as proper pairs to the decontaminated Illumina assembly. Polypolish uses these reads for correction. Filtlong also uses them when parameters.hybrid.short_read_guidance: true; that guidance is disabled by default. Kept, not temporary — deleting them would force the whole short-read half to re-run. {sample}/ont/{sample}_filt.fastq filter_long_reads The Oxford Nanopore reads Filtlong kept — what Flye assembled and what Medaka polished with. {sample}/ont/raw_qc/, {sample}/ont/filt_qc/ raw_long_read_qc, filtered_long_read_qc NanoPlot read-length and quality profiles, before and after filtering: {sample}_NanoPlot-report.html, one interactive HTML file per plot, and {sample}_NanoStats.txt. Read side by side: the difference is what the filter did. The plots are HTML only, with no PNG copies, because NanoPlot needs a Chrome browser on the machine to draw static images.

The trimmed Illumina pairs ({sample}_trim_R{1,2}.fastq) are temporary and are gone when the run finishes. 01.reads/phix/ is kept: the PhiX genome, phix.fna.gz, fetched once, and the six Bowtie2 index files built from it, phix.*.bt2, about 8 MB, built once. The index is kept so that a sample added to the output folder later runs on its own: built again, it would make every finished sample redo its PhiX screen and everything after it, the assembly included (What survives between runs). See Illumina mode and Nanopore mode.

docs.title: 02.assembly — the genome and everything used to judge it
The delivered genome
docs.text:
02.assembly/{sample}/contigs_final.fasta is the one hand-off between the front end and everything after it. Every rule in stages 03 to 08 works from this file or from something built out of it, so nothing downstream has to know which assembler ran. The one deliberate exception is hybrid, where QUAST, CheckM and GTDB-Tk are also handed the Illumina assembly as a comparator — see eval/ below.

What it is differs by mode:

Mode contigs_final.fasta is Also kept illumina the decontaminated SPAdes assembly — decontamination is the last assembly step contigs_filt.fasta, the pre-decontamination draft contigs the decontaminated input assembly contigs_filt.fasta nanopore the Medaka consensus of the decontaminated, reoriented Flye assembly contaminants/assembly_decontam.fasta hybrid the Oxford Nanopore assembly after Medaka and Polypolish contaminants/contigs_sel.fasta, the decontaminated Illumina assembly, kept as the QC comparator and as Snippy's reference

Set parameters.{nanopore,hybrid}.medaka_model: false and the consensus step drops out of the last two rows: nanopore then delivers the decontaminated reoriented assembly as it stands, hybrid delivers the reoriented Flye assembly after Polypolish alone; its final decontamination screen remains advisory.

In contigs mode, what contigs_filt.fasta holds depends on the headers you fed in. The length and coverage filter reads both numbers out of the header itself, so it can only run on SPAdes-style headers: those keep their names and lose any contig under 500 bp or 2× coverage. Any other header style has no numbers to read, so nothing is filtered and the headers are trimmed to their first token instead. Which branch ran is the first line of logs/filter_contigs_{sample}.log.

In hybrid the contamination screen runs on the Illumina draft while the delivered genome comes from the Oxford Nanopore analysis, so those two FASTAs have entirely different contig names. That is not a bug and it is why the plasmid step gets its own BLAST table (below).

docs.title: contaminants/
docs.text:
The contamination screen and its audit trail, all under 02.assembly/{sample}/contaminants/.

File Contents {sample}_blastout The megablast table over the draft assembly: 15 tab-separated columns with the subject title last. {sample}_final_blastout [nanopore, hybrid] A second megablast, over contigs_final.fasta. It exists because the plasmid step looks contigs up by ID, and in the long-read modes the screened contigs and the delivered contigs do not share names. bestscore.blob.blobDB.table.txt The BlobTools per-contig table — taxonomy and coverage. The evidence behind every keep/drop decision, so it is kept. contig_taxonomy_decisions.tsv The audit file. Every contig, its assigned genus, and the reason it was kept or dropped. contigs.list The kept contig IDs, one per line. {sample}_composition.txt One line per genus with its share of the DNA (bp) and of the contig count (contigs), over every contig in the BlobTools table — kept or dropped. A report to read; no later step reads it. {sample}_kept_genus.txt One line: the genus of the kept contigs, by default the kept genus holding the most DNA. The annotation step gives it to Bakta as the organism's genus. Empty when no kept contig has a genus. {sample}_final_contig_taxonomy_decisions.tsv, {sample}_final_composition.tsv, bestscore_final.blob_final.blobDB.table.txt [hybrid] The second screen, of the delivered genome: a verdict per contig under parameters.decontamination.long_read_mode, its composition report, and its BlobTools table. A check only; contigs_final.fasta is not changed by it.

blob.blobDB.json, the coverage file beside it, and the alignment BAM are all temporary. Full reasoning, and the two routes by which this step can delete a real plasmid, on Decontamination.

docs.title: eval/
docs.text:
Path Contents {sample}_qc_genomes.tsv Which genome is which: bin id, role (primary or comparator), technology, source path. In hybrid this is the file that says which of the two rows is the delivered genome. quast/ QUAST assembly metrics — contig count, N50, largest contig, total length, GC. checkm/{sample}_checkm_stats.tsv CheckM completeness and contamination. lineage.ms beside it is CheckM's own marker-set file. qualimap/ Coverage depth and evenness of the reads on the assembly. Absent in contigs mode, where the only alignment is the contigs against themselves and a report on it would say nothing.

In hybrid, QUAST, CheckM and GTDB-Tk each run over two genomes per sample — {sample}_illumina and {sample}_ont — so one report holds both and the comparison is the point. The staging directory eval/genomes/ that carries them there is temporary. See Assembly QC.

docs.title: Front-end working directories
docs.text:
Kept as the assembler left them, for when you need to see what happened.

Directory Modes Contents spades/ [illumina, hybrid] SPAdes' own output, including contigs.fasta before the length and coverage filter. flye/ [nanopore, hybrid] assembly.fasta, Flye's assembly_info.txt (which carries the circularity call), and ignore_list.txt — the contigs Flye did not close, which dnaapler must not rotate. fix_start/ [nanopore, hybrid] dnaapler's reoriented assembly, the header-trimmed copy, and the reorientation summary. medaka/ [nanopore, hybrid] consensus.fasta and Medaka's working files. Absent when Medaka is switched off. polypolish/ [hybrid] Empty at the end — every file in it is temporary. snps/ [hybrid] One numbered sub-directory per Snippy run — 01.flye_snps_dir through 04.polypolish_snps_dir — each comparing one Oxford Nanopore stage against the Illumina assembly, plus SNPs_summary.txt. With Medaka off, 03 holds a skipped.txt instead of a comparison. {sample}_replicons.tsv [nanopore, hybrid] The five-column table handed to Bakta as --replicons: topology from Flye, replicon type from dnaapler. {sample}_replicons_audit.tsv beside it carries the raw numbers and a reason per contig. {sample}_medaka_model.txt [nanopore, hybrid] The Medaka model that was confirmed or inferred, written early so a bad model fails in seconds rather than after the assembler has run. Absent when Medaka is switched off, along with the rule that writes it.

docs.title: 03.taxonomy — GTDB-Tk
docs.text:
One directory per sample, named by GTDB-Tk itself. The file to read is classify/gtdbtk.bac120.summary.tsv (gtdbtk.ar53.summary.tsv for archaea): the placement, the closest reference and the ANI to it.

MultiQC reads that summary, and — when the mobilome module is on — so does the step that maps the species to an AMRFinderPlus --organism, which is what unlocks point-mutation detection. See Taxonomy.

docs.title: 04.annotation
docs.text:
Path Contents bakta/{sample}/ The full Bakta annotation set — {sample}.gff3, .tsv, .faa, .fna, .gbff and more. Three later stages reach into this directory: eggNOG takes the .faa, antiSMASH the .gbff, dbCAN both the .faa and the .gff3. eggnog/{sample}/ {sample}.emapper.* — orthologous group per protein, with COG category, GO, KEGG KO and pathway, EC. Terminal: nothing else reads it. antismash/{sample}/ Secondary-metabolite clusters, with antiSMASH's own HTML report. Terminal. antismash/databases/ The shared antiSMASH reference database: downloaded here, or a symlink view of a copy you already hold. dbcan/{sample}/ CAZyme calls, gene clusters and substrate predictions. Terminal. dbcan/<db version>/ The shared dbCAN database, likewise. The folder is named from the download URL, so the version is visible on disk. The empty .verified.sha256 beside it is the marker written once the checksum matched, and its presence is what stops the download repeating.

eggNOG is the slow tail of a BacFlux run. See Annotation.

docs.title: 05.amr
docs.text: The assembly-based ABRicate screen runs in every mode. Illumina and hybrid modes also map reads against CARD. These analyses use different inputs and detection criteria, so disagreement should be investigated rather than treated as an error.

docs.title: abricate/{sample}/
docs.text: One TSV per database — argannot, card, ecoh, ecoli_vf, megares, ncbi, resfinder, vfdb — plus AMR_summary.txt, which collates a sample's eight tables. This analysis carries the EFSA thresholds: a hit needs ≥80% identity and ≥70% gene-length coverage.

docs.title: mapping/{sample}/ — [illumina, hybrid]
docs.text:
Trimmed reads mapped onto CARD's protein homolog model. Read mapping can detect sequence not recovered in the assembly, but coverage, related references and ambiguous mapping affect the result.

File Contents {sample}_CARD_report.tsv The one to read. One row per CARD sequence that cleared the coverage gate, with CARD's own classification joined on: aro_accession, aro_name, covered_percent, category, resistance_mechanism, amr_gene_family, drug_class, reference_organism, note. category is what stops an efflux-pump subunit being counted as an acquired resistance gene. {sample}_covstats.tsv BBMap's raw coverage table, sorted by descending covered percent. The evidence behind the report. {sample}_AMR_legend.tsv Every feature covered ≥70%, with its row from CARD's aro_index.tsv.

What this analysis is actually screened at

BBMap is passed minid=0.76, its own default (CARD_MIN_IDENTITY in workflow/rules/shared/00_common.smk). Read this as a sensitive screen: its specificity comes from requiring reads to cover at least 70% of the reference gene's length (CARD_MIN_COVERED, same file), not from per-read identity.

05.amr/card_db/ holds the CARD database this run used — downloaded there, or a symlink view of the copy at directories.card_db. Either way it is kept, so CARD is fetched once per output folder. See Antimicrobial resistance.

docs.title: 06.plasmids
docs.text:
Path Contents {sample}/platon/verified_plasmids.txt The terminal plasmid product on the default path: the contigs Platon called plasmid, each annotated with whether its best nucleotide hit also says "plasmid". That check is supplementary and never a filter — a mobile element on a genuinely chromosomal contig can push both signals the same wrong way. {sample}/platon/contigs_final.tsv Platon's per-contig table with its replicon-distribution score. Platon names every file after the input basename, hence contigs_final.*. {sample}/platon/contigs_final.chromosome.fasta The contigs Platon called chromosome. {sample}/{sample}_plasmid_concordance.tsv Optional. Written only when phage.caller: genomad. One row per contig joining Platon's call and geNomad's, with a confidence column: both callers agree → high, one only → medium, a real clash → low. Nothing is dropped; a disagreement is flagged and kept.

See Plasmids.

docs.title: 07.phages
docs.text:
Which caller runs is set by phage.caller, and the choice changes what stage 06 holds as well as this one.

Path Contents virsorter/{sample}/ Default. VirSorter2's calls at a deliberately loose score cutoff of 0.5; the file CheckV grades is final-viral-combined.fa. genomad/{sample}/ Only when opted in. One geNomad run produces both the virus calls (contigs_final_summary/contigs_final_virus.fna) and the plasmid calls (contigs_final_summary/contigs_final_plasmid_summary.tsv) that stage 06's concordance table needs. checkv/{sample}/quality_summary.tsv The phage deliverable. Completeness, contamination and a quality tier per predicted viral sequence. A genome with no viral calls gets a header-only file rather than a failed run. vs2_db/, genomad_db/, checkv_db/ The caller's and CheckV's databases. Each is either downloaded here or built as a symlink view of a copy you already hold — BacFlux only ever reads your copy.

See Prophages.

docs.title: 08.mobilome — opt-in
docs.text:
Written only when mobilome.run: true. That adds ten rules on the default path; the module's other twelve belong to four optional layers, each of which stays off until you configure a source for it. See Enabling the module.

Databases and model sets sit at the top of the stage, fetched once and shared by every sample: conjscan_models/, and — each only when its layer is configured — icescan_models/, tncentral_db/, iceberg_db/, isosdb_db/.

Per sample, 08.mobilome/{sample}/ holds:

File Contents {sample}_amr_mobility.tsv The deliverable. One row per AMR gene: its mobile-element context, the element's identity where one is known, the contig-edge flags, a mobility tier from 1 to 6 and a confidence. {sample}_amr_mobility_audit.tsv Why every gene that got no context got none. {sample}_is_summary.tsv The contig-boundary summary: how many insertion-sequence calls sit within mobilome.contig_boundary_bp of a contig end, and what fraction of the total that is. Read this before the table above. {sample}_is_elements.tsv, {sample}_is_discarded.tsv One row per insertion-sequence prediction, and the dropped rows with a reason — among them overlaps_dnaA, a call lying over the essential gene dnaA, and overlaps_helicase_loader, a partial IS21 lying over the chromosome's own helicase loader (dnaC or dnaI with its chromosomal partner beside it and no IS21 transposase near it). ISEScan reports both because its IS21 profiles also match DnaA and the loader, ATPases of the same family as the IS21 helper protein IstB. Neither call is an insertion: both genes are essential. {sample}_ice_candidates.tsv, {sample}_ice_discarded.tsv ICE/IME candidates with their anchors, boundaries and class; and the discard trail. {sample}_amrfinderplus.tsv, _amrfinderplus_mutations.tsv The AMR calls with coordinates and a method column; point mutations separately. {sample}_amrfinder_organism.txt, _amrfinder_organism_audit.tsv Which AMRFinderPlus --organism the GTDB-Tk placement mapped to, or none, and why. {sample}_replicon_calls.tsv Chromosome or plasmid, per contig, with the evidence for the call. {sample}_contig_lengths.tsv The yardstick every contig-edge flag is measured against. isescan/, conjscan/ The tools' own output trees, kept as raw evidence. icescan/ joins them when that optional second model set is switched on. {sample}_named_elements.tsv, {sample}_named_elements_discarded.tsv, {sample}_tncentral_blast.tsv Optional. Curated transposons and integrons — the layer that makes tier 4 reachable. {sample}_ice_candidates_named.tsv, {sample}_ice_naming.tsv, {sample}_iceberg_blast.tsv Optional. Curated names put on the ICE/IME candidates. Labels only: this layer cannot change any gene's tier. {sample}_is_copy_number.tsv, {sample}_is_copy_number_audit.tsv, {sample}_isosdb_covstats.tsv, {sample}_assembly_covstats.tsv Optional, [illumina, hybrid]. IS copy numbers estimated from read depth and compared with the located calls; the difference estimates the copies the assembly collapsed rather than counting them.

conjscan_output_missing means the search did not run

An ICE/IME search that ran and found no conjugation machinery above the reporting thresholds, and a search that did not run, both leave the results table without calls.

They are distinguished in {sample}_ice_discarded.tsv. If it carries the reason conjscan_output_missing, the expected search output was unavailable: read the absence of ICE and IME calls as unknown, not as absence. This is the same distinction the mobility ladder makes between not_assessable and tier 1.

Every column of the mobility table, with real rows, is on Reading the output. What fragmentation does to a call, and what not to conclude from one, is on Draft assemblies.

docs.title: 09.report
docs.text:
File Contents multiqc_report.html fastp or NanoPlot, Qualimap, QUAST, CheckM, GTDB-Tk and Bakta for the whole batch, with sample names rewritten into readable panel labels. multiqc_config.yaml The generated config, kept so the renaming rules are inspectable. multiqc_data/ MultiQC's parsed numbers behind the report.

Left alone, MultiQC names a sample after every directory component of the file it came from. The generated config rewrites those into <what it is> | <sample> — so a panel row reads assembly QC | S1, and a hybrid sample's two genomes appear separately as completeness Illumina | S1 and completeness ONT | S1.

The report directory is deliberately not a declared Snakemake output, so anything you drop in it survives a re-run.

docs.title: logs
docs.text:
One file per rule invocation, flat, with the sample appended where the rule runs per sample — logs/annotation_S1.log, logs/multiqc.log. The stem is usually the rule's own name, but not always: every mobilome rule logs under a mobilome_ prefix, so rule isescan writes logs/mobilome_isescan_S1.log, and a handful elsewhere are shortened — map_amr_db writes logs/map_amr_S1.log. The log is the first place to look when a rule fails, and the only place some warnings go: the decontamination selector's "N contigs from the BlobTools table were not found in the FASTA", for instance, is written there rather than to the console.

There is no benchmarks/ directory: no rule declares Snakemake's benchmark: directive, so the workflow does not produce per-rule benchmark files. Tool logs or scheduler records may still contain timing or memory information.

docs.title: Temporary files, and directories a re-run wipes
docs.text:
Some outputs are declared temporary: Snakemake deletes them as soon as every rule that needed them has finished. They are absent from a completed run, which is normal and not a failure.

Gone by the end Why it existed 01.reads/{sample}/illumina/{sample}.{1,2}.fastq and {sample}_trim_R{1,2}.fastq The PhiX-free pairs and then the fastp-trimmed pairs. The trimmed ones survive until the last rule that reads them is done: the assembler, the coverage alignment, the CARD analysis, and in hybrid the mapping that picks the Illumina pairs to keep. 02.assembly/{sample}/contaminants/{sample}_map.bam, the BlobTools JSON and coverage file Intermediates of the screen; the BlobTools table is kept. 02.assembly/{sample}/eval/genomes/ Staging copies of the assemblies under their bin ids, for QUAST, CheckM and GTDB-Tk. 02.assembly/{sample}/polypolish/ contents Alignments and the pre-correction draft. 04.annotation/eggnog/{sample}_tmp/ emapper's scratch space. 05.amr/card.tar.bz2, on the download path The downloaded CARD archive, removed once it is unpacked into 05.amr/card_db/, which is kept. 08.mobilome/{sample}/assembly_depth_ref/, isosdb_ref/ BBMap indexes for the copy-number analysis. 09.report/multiqc_inputs/ Relabelled CheckM and GTDB-Tk copies staged for MultiQC.

Nearly every tool directory on this page is a declared Snakemake directory output: the per-sample trees written by Bakta, eggNOG, antiSMASH, dbCAN, QUAST, CheckM, Qualimap, GTDB-Tk, Platon, the phage caller, CheckV, ISEScan and CONJscan, and every database directory the workflow fetches. Snakemake deletes a directory output before re-running the rule that makes it, so anything you put inside one will not survive that rule re-running. Keep your own files beside them, not in them. 09.report/ is the deliberate exception, although keeping your own analysis files outside generated outputs is easier to manage.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Configuration — every key referred to above, and its default.
  • Running BacFlux — dry runs, --cores, and what a re-run rebuilds.
  • Reference databases — which databases you supply and which the workflow fetches into the output directory.
  • Troubleshooting — an empty or missing output, and what it usually means.

docs.title: Running BacFlux
docs.text:
One command runs all four modes. Which pipeline you get is decided by mode: inside the config file, not on the command line, so the launch line looks the same for an Illumina batch and for a folder of finished assemblies.

conda activate snakemake
cd /path/to/BacFlux

# check what would run, without running it
snakemake --sdm conda --cores 24 --configfile config/config_custom.yaml -n

# launch
snakemake --sdm conda --cores 24 --configfile config/config_custom.yaml

config/config_custom.yaml is your own copy of the shipped example (cp config/config.yaml config/config_custom.yaml), git-ignored so your edits survive a git pull. See Quick start.

Terms used on this page

DAG directed acyclic graph — the job graph Snakemake builds from the rules, which decides what runs and in what order RAM the machine's memory, as opposed to disk CPU a processor core, the unit --cores counts OOM out of memory — a job killed by the system for using more than the machine had QC quality control — the read and assembly checks YAML the config file's plain-text format; indentation is significant and tabs are refused GTDB Genome Taxonomy Database, the reference GTDB-Tk places each genome in

docs.title: Launch from the repository root
docs.text:
Three things are anchored to the directory you launch from, so make it the repository root every time:

  • workflow/Snakefile is found automatically from there, which is why it never has to be named on the command line.
  • .snakemake/ is created in the launch directory. It holds the per-rule conda environments, the working-directory lock, and the metadata that decides what a re-run rebuilds. Launch from somewhere else and Snakemake builds a second copy of every environment from scratch.
  • Relative paths in the config resolve against the launch directory. BacFlux deliberately does not use Snakemake's workdir: directive, so the process never changes directory; directories.output_dir is resolved to an absolute path once at parse time and every output path is built off it (OUT in workflow/rules/shared/00_common.smk). Input directories are used as given — absolute paths are safest.

The config must be named on the command line

workflow/Snakefile declares no default configfile:. That is deliberate: Snakemake merges a hard-coded config with the one passed on the command line rather than replacing it, so a default would quietly fill in any key your copy omits — with the shipped example's empty placeholders (bakta_db: "" and friends) — and the run would carry on against a path that does not exist. Without --configfile the run stops at once:

[BacFlux] No configuration supplied. Pass one explicitly, e.g.:
  snakemake --sdm conda --cores N --configfile config/config.yaml

docs.title: Always dry-run first
docs.text:
-n (or --dry-run) resolves the workflow and prints the planned jobs without executing analysis commands. Before any job starts it checks configuration and planning conditions, among them those in the table below. It does not test tool execution, model downloads or the contents of every database:

Checked at parse time Where the check lives in 00_common.smk mode missing, or not one of the four where MODE is set phage.caller that is neither genomad nor virsorter2 where PHAGE_CALLER is set an optional directories.* database path that is not a directory, or holds something other than that database _resolve_optional_db_dir() resources.threads, ram_gb or runtime_hours that is not a whole number of 1 or more _whole_number() parameters.eggnog.dbmem: true with resources.ram_gb below 42 EGGNOG_DBMEM_GB parameters.decontamination.mode or auto_vote that is not one of its options _decontam_settings() links.card_link or links.phix_link unset in a mode that needs them where CARD_LINK and PHIX_LINK are set the input directory this mode needs, unset or not a directory _require_input_dir() a sample name containing one of * # @ % ^ / ! ? & : ; | < > or a space _check_sample_names() an Illumina R1 with no R2 beside it _require_r2_mates() in hybrid mode, a sample that has reads of only one kind the hybrid sample discovery (_missing_long, _missing_short)

Each of these stops the run before any job starts, with exit status 1, so a wrapper script, a CI job or a cluster submission sees the failure as a failure. The message begins with [BacFlux], except for a missing mode, which Python reports as a KeyError.

The same parse step prints a header naming every choice the config made. Reading it costs nothing and catches a config you did not mean to run:

Mode: contigs — Downstream analysis of bacterial whole-genome assemblies.
Phage caller: virsorter2 (default). Plasmid stage: Platon-only (geNomad off).
Decontamination mode: auto (auto_vote=bp, discard_no_hit=true).
Using CheckV database from link: 'https://zenodo.org/records/21510554/files/checkv-db-v1.5.tar.gz' (db_id='checkv-db-v1.5').
Sample BAA-2146 will be processed.

Optional parts announce themselves too: the mobilome module adds a line, and eggNOG's --dbmem prints the exact flag to add (see Memory).

docs.title: --sdm conda
docs.text:
--sdm is short for --software-deployment-method, and replaces the deprecated --use-conda. It tells Snakemake to build each rule's own environment from the YAML files in workflow/envs/ and run that rule inside it. Only Snakemake itself is installed by hand; SPAdes, Flye, Bakta, GTDB-Tk and the rest are installed by the workflow on first use. The small steps get pinned environments too: BacFlux's own Python scripts run in python.yaml, and the download steps take wget, curl, tar and the unpackers from download.yaml or from the environment of the tool they serve, while some small Unix utilities still come from the host system. See Installation for those requirements.

The environments are built once and reused. By default they land in .snakemake/conda/ under the launch directory. --conda-prefix moves them:

snakemake --sdm conda --conda-prefix ~/.bacflux-envs --cores 24 \
          --configfile config/config_custom.yaml

That is worth doing when several checkouts or several projects should share one set rather than each building its own — together they are tens of gigabytes, and building them takes a while.

Build the environments ahead of time

--conda-create-envs-only builds every environment and stops. Useful before a long run, and on machines where only the login node reaches the network (On a cluster).

docs.title: Pin files: the exact environments
docs.text:
Beside every environment file in workflow/envs/ sits a <name>.linux-64.pin.txt. It lists every package in that environment, down to the exact build, as it was when the workflow was validated. On a linux-64 machine Snakemake finds it automatically and installs from it instead of solving the yaml, so installations use the same recorded conda package builds where those packages remain available. External databases, host dependencies and pip-installed packages need their own provenance. Nothing needs configuring; the run log shows Using pinnings from ... for each one.

On any other platform the pin file is ignored and the yaml is solved fresh. The Python version and the tool version are pinned there too, so the environment is still close to the validated one, but the other packages may move.

One environment has no pin file, on purpose

dbcan is installed through pip, and a pin file is a conda package list: it cannot record pip packages, and an install made from a pin file skips the yaml's pip section entirely. That environment therefore always builds from its yaml. The comment at the top of dbcan.yaml says the same, so nobody regenerates a pin file for it.

To regenerate a pin file after deliberately changing an environment, validate the rebuilt environment first, then:

conda list --explicit -p <path to the built environment> > workflow/envs/<name>.linux-64.pin.txt

docs.title: --cores is the CPU budget
docs.text:
For local execution, --cores N sets the CPU budget used by Snakemake. Every rule that wants more than one core declares Snakemake's built-in threads:, which is the directive --cores enforces automatically; the two ABRicate rules declare none and count as one core each. Rules whose tool stops scaling ask for less, through capped_cpus(n), which is min(resources.threads, n) against the config value (capped_cpus() in 00_common.smk):

Thread request Rules CPUS (the full resources.threads) map_phix, illumina_assembly (SPAdes), ont_assembly (Flye), map_contigs, map_sel_contigs, map_final_contigs capped_cpus(24) BLAST screening, QUAST, CheckM, Qualimap, GTDB-Tk, Bakta, eggNOG, antiSMASH, dbCAN, BBMap→CARD, Platon, VirSorter2, geNomad, CheckV, Polypolish, Snippy, fix_start, Medaka in nanopore mode capped_cpus(16) trim_adapters (fastp); the mobilome depth and ISOSDB mapping analyses capped_cpus(8) NanoPlot raw and filtered QC; Medaka in hybrid mode (the two long-read modes carry different values, kept as they were until timings say otherwise); the mobilome tool rules (AMRFinderPlus, ISEScan, CONJScan, ICEscan, the two BLAST naming analyses); the two CheckV database rules capped_cpus(4) virsorter2_db

So --cores 24 gives each rule its declared cap, and --cores 8 caps every request at 8 by itself — except virsorter2_db, whose own lower cap of 4 correctly wins. Lowering --cores is how you run fewer heavy jobs side by side.

Never add --jobs alongside --cores

For a local run --jobs/-j is an alias for --cores, not a second, independent "N jobs of M cores each" setting — a natural but wrong assumption. Passing both switches the core budget off rather than adding a cap on top of it. Measured: two rules each declaring threads: 8, launched with --jobs 2 --cores 8, both received their full 8 threads and ran together — 16 real threads against a declared 8-core budget. The same rules with --cores 8 alone ran one at a time. --jobs belongs on cluster runs, where it caps how many jobs are queued with the scheduler at once.

No priority scheme — the DAG orders the rules

A rule runs when its inputs exist and never before, which is the only ordering BacFlux relies on. It used to carry a priority: on 94 rules; all 94 were removed in v2.0.0. Snakemake's default scheduler maximises the sum of the priorities of the jobs it starts, unweighted by how many cores each takes, so several small per-sample jobs together outscored the one big job the numbers were meant to start first — the scheme did the opposite of its intent whenever more than a couple of jobs were ready at once.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
resources.threads and resources.ram_gb in the config describe your machine. On a single computer Snakemake enforces only the CPU side. ram_gb is handed to the tools that accept a memory ceiling, so two large jobs running at once can each take it:

Rule What ram_gb does illumina_assembly SPAdes -m, a hard ceiling it aborts rather than exceed (the rule's ram resource, in illumina/20_assembly.smk and hybrid/20_assembly.smk) map_evaluation Qualimap's Java heap, the most memory Java may use: ram_gb minus 4 GB, at most 64 GB and at least 1 GB (QUALIMAP_HEAP_GB in 00_common.smk). The 4 GB are left for what Java needs beyond its heap map_amr_db, and the mobilome depth and ISOSDB analyses BBMap -Xmx, min(ram_gb, 32) GB (the max_ram value in each rule's params:)

Three rules also declare a memory figure as a named Snakemake resource — ram on SPAdes, java_mem on Qualimap, mem_gb on eggNOG — and Snakemake schedules against a named resource only when the launch line passes it, as in --resources mem_gb=64. All three are gigabyte figures, not core counts. --resources java_mem=N also lowers each Qualimap heap to N GB, which is the way to give Qualimap less memory without lowering ram_gb for everything else.

The heavy rules also declare mem_mb and runtime, the memory and time a job asks a cluster scheduler for; on a cluster they are how ram_gb and resources.runtime_hours reach the scheduler — see On a cluster. A single computer ignores runtime, and uses mem_mb only when the launch line passes --resources mem_mb=N: each heavy step then counts as ram_gb × 1024 MB against N, so with N at or below that figure only one heavy step runs at a time.

docs.title: eggNOG --dbmem
docs.text:
eggNOG-mapper's annotation phase does random-access lookups into the 39 GB eggnog.db once per seed ortholog, which is why functional_annotation is routinely the last rule still running. Setting parameters.eggnog.dbmem: true loads that database wholly into RAM instead, at roughly 42 GB per concurrent eggNOG job (EGGNOG_DBMEM_GB in 00_common.smk). It is off by default.

Turning it on prints the flag to add, with your own ram_gb filled in:

eggNOG --dbmem is ON: each functional_annotation job loads the 39 GB eggnog.db into RAM
(~42 GB/job; 1 fit in ram_gb=64). To have Snakemake cap concurrent eggNOG jobs to that
many, add '--resources mem_gb=64' to your launch command.

snakemake --sdm conda --cores 24 --resources mem_gb=64 \
          --configfile config/config_custom.yaml

Without the flag the run still works; eggNOG concurrency then falls back to the --cores bound instead of the RAM one, which is how a machine with 64 GB ends up running two 42 GB jobs at once. Setting dbmem: true with ram_gb below 42 is refused at parse time rather than allowed to fail on the first job.

docs.title: Resuming an interrupted run
docs.text:
Snakemake rebuilds only what is missing or out of date, so an interrupted run is relaunched with the same command. Everything that finished cleanly is kept.

An interruption leaves two conditions to check.

  • Part-written outputs. A job killed mid-write leaves a file Snakemake marks incomplete. --rerun-incomplete (--ri) rebuilds those instead of trusting them.
  • A locked working directory. A run killed outright — Ctrl-C twice, a node failure, an OOM kill — can leave .snakemake/ locked. Snakemake says so on the next launch; snakemake --unlock clears it. First confirm that no run is still using the same working directory.

Changing the config can be enough to mark a step out of date on its own. Snakemake compares more than file timestamps: a changed rule parameter, script or conda environment counts too (--rerun-triggers defaults to code input mtime params software-env). A dry run answers "what would re-run?" directly, and faster than reasoning about it.

The same comparison applies after updating BacFlux. A new release changes rule code and environments, so the first run in an existing output directory plans to redo those steps and everything that depends on them, which can reach back to the assembly. Run -n first to see the plan. To keep the results you have and rebuild only what is missing or older than its inputs, add --rerun-triggers mtime to every run in that directory. Snakemake then ignores changes to rule code, parameters, input file lists and software environments, including your own configuration changes, so the directory can end up holding results made under different settings. Otherwise finish the project with the release it was started with, or use a new output directory for the updated workflow.

--ignore-incomplete and --keep-incomplete are not resume flags

They are the opposite of --rerun-incomplete: --keep-incomplete leaves a failed job's part-written output on disk, and --ignore-incomplete stops Snakemake checking for it, so that file can be accepted as a finished result. They are useful when you want to inspect what a failing rule produced. After an interruption, use --rerun-incomplete.

--keep-going (-k) is different and safe: it lets independent jobs carry on when one fails, so a whole batch is not lost to one bad sample. It applies only to runtime failures, never to a parse or DAG error.

docs.title: When a QC tool fails
docs.text:
Four tools produce reports that nothing else in the workflow reads: QUAST (assembly metrics), Qualimap (read-mapping quality), NanoPlot (long-read QC) and CheckV (prophage grading). MultiQC gathers what they wrote; no analysis step depends on them. So if one of them crashes on a sample, the rule finishes anyway: it creates its output directory first, lets the tool fail, and writes a note beginning NOTE: into that sample's log under logs/. The run carries on, and that sample simply has no section for that tool in the MultiQC report.

The reverse is deliberate too. CheckM, the genome-staging step and the assembly-depth step look like QC but feed later rules — GTDB-Tk, QUAST itself, the IS copy-number layer — so a failure there stops the run rather than letting a bad input flow downstream.

For other runtime failures, --keep-going (-k) lets independent jobs continue: when one sample's job fails, the other samples keep running to completion instead of the whole batch stopping. Fix the one sample, then resume with --rerun-incomplete.

docs.title: What survives between runs
docs.text:
Kept where Contents Cost of deleting it .snakemake/conda/ in the launch directory, or the --conda-prefix folder the per-rule environments, and the Medaka model weights stored inside the medaka one rebuilt from scratch, needs network .snakemake/ metadata what is up to date, and the lock the next run recomputes more than it needs to under output_dir the databases the workflow fetches and keeps — the PhiX genome and its Bowtie2 index, CARD, antiSMASH, dbCAN, CheckV, the phage caller's own database, and the optional mobilome databases re-downloaded or rebuilt; for PhiX and CARD, see below output_dir/logs/ one log per rule and sample (LOGS in 00_common.smk) nothing recomputes; you lose the record

The PhiX index and CARD are kept for a reason beyond saving a download. Snakemake redoes every step whose input is rebuilt, or newer than that step's results:

  • The PhiX index is read by every sample's PhiX screen. If it were deleted after each run, the next run that screens any sample in the same output folder, such as a sample added to it, would build it again, and every finished sample would redo its PhiX screen and everything after it, the assembly included.
  • CARD is read by every sample's CARD step, which works from the trimmed reads. Those are temporary, and so are the PhiX-free reads they are trimmed from. A CARD folder fetched again after a run would be newer than every finished sample's CARD result, so the next run would redo that step for each sample, and with it everything from the PhiX screen onwards, the assembly included.

Kept, PhiX and CARD are downloaded and the index built once per output folder, and a sample added to the folder later runs on its own; only the MultiQC report, which covers every sample, is made again. A folder whose 01.reads/phix/ holds no phix.*.bt2 files, for example after the archive clean-up (workflow/scripts/clean_workdir.sh) has removed them, has no index: the next run that screens a sample builds it, and every finished sample there is redone. Put new samples in a new output folder instead.

Reusing the same launch directory and the same output_dir is what keeps the rest from being rebuilt. Databases you already hold elsewhere can be pointed at instead of downloaded — see Reference databases.

docs.title: On a cluster
docs.text:
BacFlux runs on a Slurm cluster in one of two ways:

A. Snakemake sends each step to Slurm B. The whole run in one batch job Where Snakemake runs on the login node, or another node with internet, for the whole run inside one batch job, on one compute node Where the steps run each step is a Slurm job of its own, on any compute node; the download steps and the Medaka model check run where Snakemake runs all on that node Command --executor slurm --jobs N (Run A) --cores N, as on a single computer (Run B) Memory and time each heavy step asks Slurm for resources.ram_gb and resources.runtime_hours the batch job asks once, for the whole run Internet on the compute nodes not needed not needed once the preparation has run; the long-read modes need one more step for the Medaka model weights Needs the Slurm executor plugin; a login node on which Snakemake may run for many hours one node with the cores, memory and time of the whole run Checked the local rules by the test suite, and every job's requests by dry runs (-n prints them); not yet run on a Slurm cluster as on a single computer

Option A distributes jobs across nodes and runs download rules where Snakemake runs. Option B runs the workflow within one allocated node. Both start with the same preparation, and both need the same shared storage.

docs.title: Preparation, on a computer with internet
docs.text:
Run these commands from the BacFlux folder on a computer that has internet and sees the same storage as the compute nodes: the login node, or a data-transfer node.

  1. Copy the template and fill it in. Put every path on shared storage, and set resources.threads, ram_gb and runtime_hours from the limits of the cluster (table below).

    conda activate snakemake
cd /path/to/BacFlux
cp config/config.yaml config/config_custom.yaml

  2. Build the conda environments of every step of the run. Some of them fetch data while they are built — CheckM's reference data, for one — so this step needs internet too. conda first downloads every package into its package cache, by default inside the conda installation; if that sits in a home folder with a small quota, move the cache to project space first, as in the first line:

    export CONDA_PKGS_DIRS=/path/to/project_space/conda_pkgs
snakemake --sdm conda --conda-prefix /path/to/project_space/bacflux_envs \
    --conda-create-envs-only --configfile config/config_custom.yaml

  3. Fetch everything BacFlux downloads itself, and nothing else. Add -n first to see the plan.

    snakemake download_all --sdm conda --conda-prefix /path/to/project_space/bacflux_envs \
    --cores 4 --configfile config/config_custom.yaml

  4. Check. The dry run must print Nothing to be done (all requested files are present and up to date).

    snakemake download_all -n --sdm conda --conda-prefix /path/to/project_space/bacflux_envs \
    --configfile config/config_custom.yaml
Rule Why Write download_all right after snakemake. --configfile and --sdm each take one or more values, so at the end of the line download_all is read as one of them and Snakemake stops with an error. Run steps 2 to 4 and the real run from the same folder, with the same configuration and the same --conda-prefix. Relative paths in the configuration are read from the launch folder, and Snakemake keeps its records in .snakemake/ there. Without --conda-prefix the environments are in that .snakemake/conda/ too. Snakemake also records where each step's environment was, so with another prefix the real run builds the environments again and runs every download step again (reason Software environment definition has changed since last execution). Run steps 2 to 4 again after any change to the configuration. A short-read mode adds PhiX and CARD, the other phage caller adds its own database, and each mobilome layer switched on adds its own.

Behind a proxy that re-signs HTTPS traffic, point both SSL_CERT_FILE and REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE at your site's certificate file before starting Snakemake. The download tools check servers against the certificate list in their conda environment, not the computer's: wget and curl read SSL_CERT_FILE, and the Python downloaders, among them Medaka's download of its model weights, read REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE.

What download_all fetches, according to the configuration:

Download Rule When Where it lands, under output_dir PhiX genome download_phix illumina, hybrid 01.reads/phix/phix.fna.gz. Only the genome: its Bowtie2 index is built beside it by the first run that screens reads (build_phix), which needs no internet CARD download_amr_db illumina, hybrid, unless directories.card_db names your copy 05.amr/card_db/ dbCAN database cazyme_db_download unless directories.dbcan_db names your copy 04.annotation/dbcan/<release>/ antiSMASH databases secondary_metabolites_db unless directories.antismash_db names your copy 04.annotation/antismash/databases/ VirSorter2 database virsorter2_db phage.caller: virsorter2, unless directories.vs2_db names your copy 07.phages/vs2_db/ geNomad database genomad_db phage.caller: genomad, unless directories.genomad_db names your copy 07.phages/genomad_db/ CheckV database checkv_db unless directories.checkv_db names your copy 07.phages/checkv_db/ CONJScan models conjscan_models mobilome.run 08.mobilome/conjscan_models/ ICEscan models icescan_models mobilome.icescan.run 08.mobilome/icescan_models/ TnCentral tncentral_db the tncentral layer is on 08.mobilome/tncentral_db/ ICEberg iceberg_db the iceberg layer is on 08.mobilome/iceberg_db/ ISOSDB isosdb_db the isosdb layer is on, in illumina and hybrid 08.mobilome/isosdb_db/

download_all leaves out two things. The five databases you provide yourself (bakta_db, blast_db, eggnog_db, gtdbtk_db, platon_db) are named by path and never downloaded by the workflow (Reference databases). And the Medaka model weights are fetched during the run, by the model check — see below. The list itself is download_targets() in 00_common.smk.

docs.title: Run A: Snakemake sends each step to Slurm
docs.text:
Install the Slurm executor plugin once into the launcher environment:

conda activate snakemake
conda install -c conda-forge -c bioconda snakemake-executor-plugin-slurm

Then, on the login node, start Snakemake inside screen or tmux, so that it keeps running when you log out:

snakemake --executor slurm --jobs 20 --latency-wait 60 --sdm conda \
    --conda-prefix /path/to/project_space/bacflux_envs \
    --default-resources slurm_account=<account> slurm_partition=<partition> mem_mb=8000 runtime=240 \
    --configfile config/config_custom.yaml
Option What it does --executor slurm submits every step to Slurm with sbatch, except the local rules: the download steps and check_medaka_model run on the login node --jobs 20 the most jobs Snakemake keeps queued or running at once; it refuses to start without --jobs --latency-wait 60 after a job ends, Snakemake waits up to 60 seconds for its files to appear on the login node. Shared storage can show a file written on a compute node only some seconds later, and the default wait, 5 seconds, is often too short --default-resources the values for every job that does not set its own: the account and partition for every job (leave them out if your cluster needs none), memory (MB) and time (minutes) for the light steps. A rule's own value wins over it

--cores is not needed: resources.threads already caps the CPUs of each job. Given together with --executor, it does not cap the jobs' total; it lowers each job's threads to at most that number, and the job then asks Slurm for that many.

The local rules run on the login node with their own thread counts, and Snakemake 9.14.6 has no setting that limits them there. The heaviest is the CheckV download, which builds a DIAMOND index with up to 8 threads. Running the preparation first means every download is done before the run starts, so during the run the only local step is the Medaka model check.

Each Slurm job writes a log of its own under .snakemake/slurm_logs/ in the launch folder, and when a job fails the Error in rule block names that file. The messages of the tool itself are in logs/ of the output folder, as on a single computer.

docs.title: How the settings reach Slurm
docs.text:
Setting Each job asks Slurm for Must not exceed Shown by resources.threads --cpus-per-task: the threads of its step, at most this number (the thread table under --cores above) the CPUs of one compute node sinfo -o "%n %c" resources.ram_gb --mem: ram_gb × 1024 MB for every heavy step (table below) the memory Slurm offers one compute node sinfo -o "%n %m", in MB: divide by 1024 and round down resources.runtime_hours -t: runtime_hours × 60 minutes for every heavy and every long step the time limit of the partition sinfo -o "%P %l" --default-resources mem_mb=... runtime=... --mem and -t for the light steps the same limits the same commands Steps Memory asked for Time asked for the heavy steps: SPAdes (illumina_assembly), Flye (ont_assembly), Medaka (long_read_consensus), Polypolish (short_read_correction), the read mappings of decontamination (map_contigs in the read-based modes, map_final_contigs), the BLAST screens (blast_contigs, blast_final_contigs), CheckM (completeness_and_contamination), GTDB-Tk (taxonomic_assignment), Bakta (annotation), eggNOG-mapper (functional_annotation), antiSMASH (secondary_metabolites_analysis), BBMap against CARD (map_amr_db), geNomad (genomad_end_to_end), VirSorter2 (viral_identification_virsorter2), and the two read mappings of the mobilome module (assembly_depth, isosdb_map) ram_gb runtime_hours Qualimap (map_evaluation) its Java heap plus 4 GB, never more than ram_gb (Memory) runtime_hours the long steps that hold little in memory: the PhiX filter (map_phix) and the read selection of hybrid (map_sel_contigs) nothing runtime_hours every other step nothing nothing

The figures come from HEAVY_MEM_MB, QUALIMAP_JOB_MB and LONG_RUNTIME_MINUTES in 00_common.smk, and a dry run prints each job's requests.

Set threads, ram_gb and runtime_hours so that one job fits one node and one partition. GTDB-Tk alone needs about 55 GB, so give ram_gb at least about 60. A ram_gb well below the node's memory lets several heavy jobs share a node.

  • A step that asks for nothing gets Slurm's defaults, often a GB or two per CPU and the partition's default time. If those are smaller than a few GB or an hour, give --default-resources mem_mb=8000 runtime=240 as above, and raise it if a light step is stopped for memory or time.
  • Changing threads or runtime_hours re-runs nothing. Changing ram_gb re-runs the BBMap steps when min(ram_gb, 32) changes with it, because that number is one of their parameters. In illumina and hybrid that reaches much further: the trimmed reads those steps read are temporary, so Snakemake trims the reads again, and everything that reads them runs again too, the assembly included. Settle ram_gb before the first run.

docs.title: Run B: the whole run in one batch job
docs.text:
Step What to do Request one node with N cores and enough memory: at least resources.ram_gb, which SPAdes takes as its ceiling and Qualimap sizes its heap from, and at least about 60 GB, because GTDB-Tk needs 55 GB Configure resources.threads: N, the number of cores you request Prepare when the node has no internet: the preparation above, on the login node, with the folder and --conda-prefix of the batch script; in the long-read modes also the Medaka step Launch inside the job, from the same folder, the usual command with --cores N (script below) Time limit the whole run, plus the building of the environments and the downloads when they were not prepared. After a job is stopped at its time limit, submit the same script again (Resuming an interrupted run); if Snakemake asks for --unlock, run the command once with it first

Treat the allocated node as a single computer. On one node Snakemake counts only threads: resources.ram_gb is then only the memory ceiling of SPAdes, the size of the Qualimap heap and the cap of BBMap, and runtime_hours is ignored.

docs.title: A batch script
docs.text:
For Slurm; other schedulers take the same commands with their own resource lines. Save it as bacflux.sbatch and submit it with sbatch bacflux.sbatch.

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=bacflux
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=24      # N: the same number as resources.threads
#SBATCH --mem=128G              # at least resources.ram_gb (Request row above)
#SBATCH --time=24:00:00         # Time limit row above

# Make "conda activate" work inside a batch job, then activate Snakemake.
eval "$(conda shell.bash hook)"
conda activate snakemake

cd /path/to/BacFlux
# --rerun-incomplete: rebuild what a time limit cut short, when the job is resubmitted.
snakemake --sdm conda --conda-prefix /path/to/project_space/bacflux_envs \
    --cores "$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK" --rerun-incomplete \
    --configfile config/config_custom.yaml

$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK holds the number of cores Slurm gave the job, so --cores always matches the request.

docs.title: Medaka model weights without internet
docs.text:
In nanopore and hybrid mode the Medaka model check, rule check_medaka_model, finds the model and fetches its weights during the run. It is a local rule: in Run A it runs on the login node, where there is internet, and nothing more is needed. download_all cannot fetch the weights ahead of the run, because the check reads the filtered long reads to identify the model, and those exist only once the run has filtered them.

So in Run B, on a node without internet, run the workflow once up to the check, on the login node, from the same folder and with the same --conda-prefix:

snakemake --until check_medaka_model --sdm conda \
    --conda-prefix /path/to/project_space/bacflux_envs \
    --cores 4 --configfile config/config_custom.yaml

That filters the long reads there (Filtlong, one core per sample; in hybrid with short_read_guidance: true the Illumina steps before it run too), checks the model and stores its weights in the medaka environment, where the batch job finds them. The other way is to switch polishing off, with medaka_model: false.

docs.title: Shared storage
docs.text:
Must be on storage every compute node sees, under the same path Why the BacFlux folder and the launch folder, with its .snakemake/ every job reads the workflow and Snakemake's records the conda installation, with the launcher environment in it in A, each job starts Snakemake again with the same Python, and Snakemake switches to each step's environment with that installation's activate script; in B, the batch script activates it the --conda-prefix folder every step runs in its environment from there the output folder every step reads and writes it every path in the configuration: the input folders, the five databases you provide, any directories.* database copy, the decontamination files the steps read them; in A every job also runs the start-up checks again, which look at these paths your home folder, when Medaka could not write into its environment Medaka then keeps the weights in ~/.medaka/data

On many clusters, project storage and the home directory provide these shared paths.

  • Put the environments on project space with one --conda-prefix, not on a home folder with a small quota: together they are tens of gigabytes. export CONDA_PKGS_DIRS=/path/to/project_space/conda_pkgs moves conda's package cache there too.
  • Launch every run of a project from the same folder: the environments, and the records of what is up to date, are tied to the launch folder and the prefix.

docs.title: Cleaning up a finished project
docs.text:
workflow/scripts/clean_workdir.sh strips a finished output directory down to results, reports and audit trails, deleting bulky intermediates (trimmed and filtered reads, SPAdes and Flye working directories, Medaka scratch, CheckM scratch) and every database the workflow keeps in the output tree. Raw input reads are never touched — they are read in place, never copied into the output tree.

# preview — this is what --run would delete
workflow/scripts/clean_workdir.sh /path/to/output_dir

# actually delete
workflow/scripts/clean_workdir.sh --run /path/to/output_dir

It is dry-run by default; only --run deletes, and the listing printed is identical in both modes, so the preview is exactly what you get. It recognises the current layout and the four older ones it replaced, so output directories made before v2.0.0 can still be cleaned — see Coming from v1.

This is an archive step, not a between-runs tidy

It is deliberately aggressive. Re-running the workflow on a cleaned directory recomputes a great deal, assembly and polishing included. Run it once the results are known good and you are ready to archive or hand over.

--include-snakemake additionally deletes a .snakemake/ directory found inside the output directory — which only exists if you launched from in there rather than from the repository root. It is opt-in because it is categorically heavier than the rest: that directory holds the conda environments, routinely the largest single item in a finished project. When one is present but not opted into, the script prints its size rather than quietly leaving it.

miscellaneous/clean_workdir.sh still works

It is a wrapper that forwards every argument to the real script, kept because older notes and habits point at that path.

docs.title: For contributors
docs.text:
Every script a rule runs lives in a directory named after the rule file that runs it — workflow/scripts/50_amr/ is run by workflow/rules/shared/50_amr.smk, and so on — with each test beside its script. A script sitting loose in workflow/scripts/ is not part of a run; it is a maintenance tool you run by hand, as clean_workdir.sh is. See workflow/scripts/README.md.

# the test suite: the scripts' unit tests, and the guard tests on the rule files
pytest workflow/scripts miscellaneous -q

# fail on any rule name, path, config key or constant that a comment
# mentions but that no longer exists
python miscellaneous/check_comment_references.py

docs.title: Before tagging a release
docs.text:
Run the whole workflow, not a dry run. A dry run resolves the graph and checks inputs; it never builds an environment and never executes a tool. Building the environments without running them is not enough either: a package can install cleanly and still break at runtime.

The check that catches these: a fresh clone, a fresh --conda-prefix, one small public genome, every mode. Its duration depends on the dataset and the machine. It exercises environment creation and tool execution as a new installation meets them.

The version number is declared in five places, and they have to move together:

File What to change workflow/Snakefile the header comment and the banner it prints README.md the label under the ASCII banner docs/index.md "This site documents version ..." .zenodo.json version CITATION.cff version, and date-released for the tag day

Leave every other mention of an old version alone: most of them are statements about what that release changed, and they stay true.

The oldest Snakemake BacFlux accepts is a separate number: min_version() near the top of workflow/Snakefile stops an older Snakemake at once. When it moves, move the README badge and the installation page with it.

After Zenodo archives the release, add the version DOI it mints to the identifiers block in CITATION.cff, replacing the previous version entry.
